8.text:
For the homoscedastic just identified model

${\rm RB}_{N}\equiv
{\rm plim}\frac{\widehat\beta_{2SLS}-\beta}{\widehat\beta_{OLS}-\beta}
\simeq \frac{k}{\mu^{2}}\;, \qquad k=1 ,
$

and in the weak instrument limit

$F_{1}\;\dot\sim\;\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu^{2}),\qquad 
\sqrt{F_{1}}=\sqrt{\mu^{2}}+Z+o_{p}(1),\;Z\sim N(0,1)$,
so that on the $\mu^{2}\approx F$ normalisation

${\rm RB}_{N}\simeq \mu^{-2}\simeq F^{-1} $

up to the familiar $F-1$ shift.  The mean bias point is

${\rm RB}_{N}=0.10\iff\mu^{2}_{0}=1/0.10=10$,

i.e. on the mean scale $E F\simeq1+\mu^{2}_{0}=11$ and the textbook
$1/F\simeq0.10$ rule $F_{0}\simeq10$–$11$.

Let $t_{1}=\sqrt{F_{1}}$.  Up to $o_{p}(1)$

$t_{1}\approx N\!\left(\sqrt{\mu^{2}},1\right)$

so that a one sided $95\%$ lower confidence bound for the
non-centrality is

$\sqrt{\hat\mu^{2}_{L}}=t_{1}-z_{0.95}, \qquad z_{0.95}=1.645,$

and $P\{\hat\mu^{2}_{L}\ge \mu^{2}_{0}\}=0.95$ is obtained from

$t_{1}^{*}= \sqrt{\mu^{2}_{0}}+z_{0.95}$.

With the Nagar $10\%$ point $\mu^{2}_{0}=10$,

$t_{1}^{*}= \sqrt{10}+1.645\approx3.162+1.645\approx4.81$,

i.e.

$F^{*}=t_{1}^{*2}\approx\bigl(\sqrt{10}+1.645\bigr)^{2}\approx 23.1$,

so that $F_{1}\gtrsim 23$–$24$ puts the $95\%$ one-sided lower bound
$\hat\mu^{2}_{L}=(\sqrt{F_{1}}-1.645)^{2}$ above the $10\%$ Nagar
value $\mu^{2}_{0}=10$.  On the conventional $E F=1+\mu^{2}$,
$\mu^{2}=F-1$, normalisation this is

$\sqrt{F^{*}-1}= \sqrt{10}+1.645\;\Longleftrightarrow\;
F^{*}-1\approx23.1\;\Longleftrightarrow\;F^{*}\approx24.1$,

essentially the $F\approx22$–$24$ $95\%$ lower confidence bound that is
usually quoted as the $F\approx23$ Nagar confidence bound.  Ignoring the
$+1$ shift the mean-bias point is the familiar $F_{0}\simeq1/0.10\simeq10$,
$F_{0}-1\simeq10$, i.e. the $F>10$ Staiger–Stock rule, and with the
usual Stock–Yogo size–distortion calibration the $5\%$ size $10\%$
maximal relative bias critical value is $F_{SY}(1,1)\simeq16.38\approx16$–$17$,
the $F>10$ rule inflated for sampling uncertainty. ∎

9.text:
For the just identified homoscedastic model with $k=1$ the Nagar
first order relative bias is

${\rm RB}_{N}\simeq\frac{k}{\mu^{2}},\qquad 
\mu^{2}= \frac{\pi^{\prime}Z^{\prime}Z\pi}{\sigma_{v}^{2}},$

so that on the population scale

${\rm RB}_{N}\simeq\mu^{-2}\simeq\frac{1}{F-1}\simeq\frac1F $

in large samples.  The usual $10\%$ point is therefore

$\mu_{0}^{2}=k/0.10=10$ ,   ${\rm E}F_{0}=1+\mu_{0}^{2}=11$,

the familiar $F\approx10$ rule.

For the first stage, up to $o_{p}(1)$,

$t_{1}=\sqrt{F_{1}}\;\dot\sim\;N\!\left(\sqrt{\mu^{2}},1\right)
$,
i.e. $F_{1}\dot\sim \chi^{2}_{1}(\mu^{2})=(Z+\sqrt{\mu^{2}})^{2}$.
Hence a one–sided $95\%$ lower confidence limit for $\sqrt{\mu^{2}}$
is

$\sqrt{\hat\mu^{2}_{L}}=\sqrt{F_{1}}-z_{0.95},\qquad
z_{0.95}=1.645,$

so that

$\widehat{{\rm RB}}_{U}\simeq \hat\mu_{L}^{-2}
      =\bigl(\sqrt{F_{1}}-z_{0.95}\bigr)^{-2}$.

Requiring $\widehat{{\rm RB}}_{U}\le0.10$, i.e. $\hat\mu_{L}^{2}\ge
\mu_{0}^{2}$, gives

$\sqrt{F_{1}^{*}}\ge \sqrt{\mu_{0}^{2}}+z_{0.95}$,

i.e. on the $\mu^{2}\approx F$ normalisation

$F_{1}^{*}\approx\Bigl(\sqrt{10}+1.645\Bigr)^{2}
      \approx\bigl(3.162+1.645\bigr)^{2}
      \approx 23.1\approx 23$

for a one–sided $95\%$ lower bound, $F_{1}^{*}\approx(\sqrt{10}
+1.96)^{2}\approx26$ on the two–sided $z_{0.975}$ version.  In the
conventional $E F=1+\mu^{2}$ normalisation this is
$F_{1}^{*}\approx1+(\sqrt{10}+1.645)^{2}\approx24\!-\!25$,
essentially $F_{1}\gtrsim22\!-\!24$, the textbook $F>10$ rule
inflated by the $z_{0.95}$ sampling correction.

In particular the point Nagar rule ${\rm RB}\approx1/F$ is
${\rm RB}=0.10\iff F\approx10$, $F-1\approx11$.  The finite-sample
Stock–Yogo inversion of the non-central $F$ law for a maximal $10\%$
relative bias at $5\%$ size is the familiar

$F_{SY}(1,1;{\rm rel.~bias}=0.10)\approx16.38\approx16\!-\!17$,

i.e. the $F>10$ rule quoted in practice as $F\gtrsim16$ for a
$10\%$ maximal relative bias.  This is the $F\approx23$ normal
approximation $F\approx16.4$ Stock–Yogo value quoted above. ∎

12.text:
For a just identified homoscedastic model the first order Nagar relative
bias is

${\rm RB}\approx \frac{k}{\mu^{2}}\approx\frac{1}{\mu^{2}}$,

and with $k=1$

${\rm E}F=1+\mu^{2}$  and on the usual large sample scale $F\approx\mu^{2}$
modulo the $+1$.  Up to $o_{p}(1)$

$kF\;\dot\sim\;\chi^{2}_{k}(\mu^{2}),\qquad 
\sqrt{F}=\sqrt{\mu^{2}}+Z+o_{p}(1),\;Z\sim N(0,1),$

so that on the normal scale

$\sqrt{\mu^{2}}=\sqrt{F}-Z.$

Hence a one sided $95\%$ lower confidence bound for $\sqrt{\mu^{2}}$ is
$\sqrt{\mu^{2}_{L}}=\sqrt{F}-z_{0.95}$ with $z_{0.95}=1.645$.  On the
Nagar scale ${\rm RB}\approx 1/\mu^{2}$ the $10\%$ relative bias point is

$\mu^{2}_{0}=k/0.10=10$,  $\sqrt{\mu^{2}_{0}}=\sqrt{10}\approx3.16$,

and the $95\%$ lower bound $\mu^{2}_{L}\ge\mu^{2}_{0}$ is

$\sqrt{F^{*}}-z_{0.95}\ge\sqrt{\mu^{2}_{0}}$,
i.e.

$\sqrt{F^{*}}=\sqrt{\mu^{2}_{0}}+z_{0.95}\approx
\sqrt{10}+1.645\approx4.81,$

so that on the $\mu^{2}\approx F$ normalisation

$F^{*}\approx\bigl(\sqrt{10}+1.645\bigr)^{2}\approx 23.1\approx 23$

is the $95\%$ one sided lower confidence bound for the concentration
parameter, ${\rm RB}_{L}\approx1/\mu^{2}_{L}<0.10$.  On the usual
${\rm E}F=1+\mu^{2}$ normalisation this is $F^{*}\approx1+
 (\sqrt{10}+1.645)^{2}\approx24.1$ , i.e. the familiar $F\approx22$–$26$
$95\%$ lower confidence rule, $F\approx23$–$24$ on the $\chi^{2}_{1}$
scale.  With the conventional two sided $z_{0.975}=1.96$ this is
$F^{*}\approx(\sqrt{10}+1.96)^{2}\approx26.2$.

In the $1/F$ point approximation this is the $F>1/0.10\approx10$ Staiger–
Stock rule; the Stock–Yogo maximal relative bias $5\%$ size calibration
is the usual $F_{SY}(1,1;0.10)\approx16.38\approx16$–$17$, i.e. the
$F\gtrsim10$ point rule inflated to $F\gtrsim16$ in finite sample use.

public_text.7:
I think the Nagar calculation is being conflated with the non-central chi-square quantile for the concentration parameter itself.

With homoskedasticity and k = 1

RelBias ≈ L/μ² ≈ 1/μ² ,   E F = 1 + μ²,

so on the usual F scale RelBias ≈ 1/(F-1) ≈ 1/F to first order. 
The point Nagar 10% rule is therefore 1/F ≈ 0.10 i.e. F≈10, F-1≈10
and that is the Staiger-Stock rule of thumb.

If we put a sampling error on the relative bias itself, the delta
method is the natural one.  Write r̂ = 1/F.  For large n,
Var(F) ≈ 2(1+2μ²) and with F≈1+μ²,

Var(r̂) ≈ Var(F)/F⁴ ≈ 2/F³  ,    SE(r̂)≈√2 /F^{3/2}.

A one-sided 95% upper confidence bound for the Nagar relative bias is
therefore

r_U = 1/F + z0.95 √2 /F^{3/2} < 0.10 ,

z0.95 =1.645.  With the usual 1/F normalisation this is
1/F +1.645√2 /F^{3/2} <0.10, i.e. y+1.645√2 <0.10 y³ with y=√F.
The solution is y≈4.0–4.1, i.e. F*≈15–17.  On the F-1 normalisation
r̂=1/(F-1) the same inversion gives F*≈18–20, essentially the same
operational region.

That is the finite-sample calibration that Stock and Yogo tabulate.
For L=1 endogenous and one instrument the Stock-Yogo maximal relative
bias critical value for a 5% size test is

F_{SY}(10% rel. bias,5% size, k=1)=16.38 ≈16,

commonly quoted as F≳16–17 and in round numbers F>10 on average.
It is the Nagar 1/F rule inflated for sampling uncertainty in F.

The √F≈N(√μ²,1) inversion that gives
√f* =√μ²0 +z0.95 with μ²0=10 →f*≈(3.16+1.645)²≈23.1
is a useful asymptotic normal approximation to the non-central
χ²₁(μ²) quantile, but it identifies μ² with F and it bounds μ²
rather than the ratio 1/μ².  Keeping the usual E F =1+μ² mapping the
same normal approximation is shifted upward and is essentially a
conservative large-sample limit.  In practice the Stock-Yogo finite
sample inversion is the one that is used, and it is the F≈16–17
value that is quoted as the 95% confidence, ≲10% Nagar relative bias
threshold for a just-identified homoscedastic model.  Rounded up that
is about 16-17, say 16 in the conventional tables.
public_text.13:
I think the 23-24 numbers are the one-sided 95% lower confidence bound for the concentration parameter itself, $\mu^{2}_{L}=(\sqrt{F}-z_{0.95})^{2}>10$, and that is not the same operational statement as “95% confidence that the Nagar relative bias is <10%’’.

On the Nagar first-order scale with one instrument

${\rm RB}\simeq \frac{k}{\mu^{2}}\simeq\frac{1}{F-1}\simeq\frac1F$,

and with $E[F]=1+\mu^{2}$ the point Nagar rule is
$1/(F-1)=0.10\iff F\approx11$, i.e. the familiar $F>10$ rule.

Treating the sampling uncertainty of the first-stage $F$ the usual
Stock-Yogo calibration is an inversion of the non-central $F$ distribution
for the size distortion / maximal relative bias, not an inversion of the
$(\sqrt F -z)^{2}$ lower bound for $\mu^{2}$.  Writing the relative bias as
$1/F$ and keeping the first-order sampling error,

${\rm sd}\!\left(1/F\right)\simeq\sqrt{2}/F^{3/2}$,

so that a one-sided 95% upper confidence point for the relative bias is

$\frac1F +1.645\frac{\sqrt2}{F^{3/2}}<0.10$.

That is $a^{-2}+1.645\sqrt2\,a^{-3}<0.10$ with $a=F^{1/2}$, giving
$a\approx4.0\!-\!4.1$ and $F\approx16\!-\!17$.  On the $1/(F-1)$ Nagar
normalisation this is the familiar finite-sample Stock-Yogo critical value

$F_{SY}(k=1,L=1,{\rm rel.\,bias}=0.10)\approx 16.38$,

i.e. $F\approx16$ in round numbers, $F\approx17$ if you require an
integer exceedance.  That is the operational $95\%$ confidence /
$5\%$ size maximal-relative-bias threshold that is quoted as the weak-
instrument rule, essentially the $F>10$ rule inflated for sampling
uncertainty.  The $(\sqrt{10}+1.645)^{2}\approx23$ inversion is the
conservative $95\%$ lower bound for $\sqrt{\mu^{2}}$ itself and is
systematically larger than the Stock-Yogo size-distortion calibration
which is the one normally used for the statement “the relative asymptotic
bias is <10% with $95\%$ confidence”.
public_text.2:
With the homoskedastic Nagar first order approximation for a just identified
model

${\rm E}[\hat\beta_{2SLS}-\beta]\approx 
\frac{\sigma_{uv}}{\sigma_{v}^{2}}\frac{k}{\mu^{2}} ,
\qquad 
{\rm E}[\hat\beta_{OLS}-\beta]=\frac{\sigma_{uv}}{\sigma_{v}^{2}}$ ,

so that on the population scale

$R(\mu^{2})\equiv
\frac{{\rm bias}_{2SLS}}{{\rm bias}_{OLS}}\approx\frac{k}{\mu^{2}}$ ,

and for $k=1$

$R\approx\mu^{-2}$ .

In large samples

$kF\;\dot\sim\;\chi^{2}_{k}(\mu^{2})$, $\;E F=1+\mu^{2}/k$,
and for $k=1$

$\sqrt F =\sqrt{\mu^{2}}+Z+o_{p}(1),\qquad Z\sim N(0,1)$ .

Hence a one-sided $95\%$ lower confidence bound for the concentration
parameter is

$\sqrt{\mu^{2}_{L}}=\sqrt F -z_{0.95},\qquad z_{0.95}=1.645,$

i.e. $\mu^{2}_{L}=(\sqrt F -1.645)^{2}$.  The point Nagar $10\%$ relative
bias is

$R_{0}=0.10\iff \mu^{2}_{0}=k/R_{0}=10$, $\sqrt{\mu^{2}_{0}}=\sqrt{10}$.

Requiring the lower confidence bound to still imply $R_{L}<0.10$,

$\mu^{2}_{L}\ge \mu^{2}_{0}$,

gives

$\sqrt{F^{*}}\ge \sqrt{\mu^{2}_{0}}+z_{0.95}$,

i.e.

$F^{*}\ge\bigl(\sqrt{10}+1.645\bigr)^{2}\approx
(3.162+1.645)^{2}\approx 23.1\;,$

$\approx 22\!-\!24$ on the $\mu^{2}\approx F$ normalisation.  On the
customary $E F=1+\mu^{2}$ normalisation $\mu^{2}\approx F-1$ this is

$\sqrt{F^{*}-1}\ge \sqrt{10}+1.645$,
$F^{*}\ge1+\bigl(\sqrt{10}+1.645\bigr)^{2}\approx 24.1$,

the familiar $F\gtrsim 23\!-\!25$ $95\%$ lower confidence rule.  Neglecting
the $+1$ shift the point Nagar rule is $R\approx1/F$, $F_{0}=1/R_{0}=10$,
$F_{0}-1=9\approx 11$, the textbook $F>10$ rule, which is the $F\approx
16.4$ Stock–Yogo $10\%$ maximal relative bias $5\%$ size critical value
that is normally quoted in the weak instrument tables. ∎
public_text.1:
For a just identified homoscedastic model with $k=1$

$${\rm RB}\;\approx\;\frac{{\rm E}[\hat\beta_{2SLS}-\beta]}
{{\rm E}[\hat\beta_{OLS}-\beta]}
\;\approx\;\frac{k}{\mu^{2}}\approx\frac{1}{\mu^{2}}
 \approx\frac{1}{E[F]-1}\approx\frac1F , $$

so that on the mean a $10\%$ Nagar relative bias is 
$\mu^{2}_{0}=1/0.10=10$ , i.e. $E[F]_{0}=1+\mu^{2}_{0}\approx10\!-\!11$.
In the weak instrument limit

$$F\;\dot\sim\;\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu^{2})=(Z+\sqrt{\mu^{2}})^{2},
\qquad Z\sim N(0,1), $$

so that up to $o_{p}(1)$

$$\sqrt F=\sqrt{\mu^{2}}+Z+o_{p}(1) .$$

Hence a one sided $95\%$ lower confidence bound for the non-centrality
is

$$\sqrt{\mu^{2}_{L}}=\sqrt{F_{obs}}-z_{0.95},\qquad 
z_{0.95}=1.645, $$

i.e. $\mu^{2}_{L} =(\sqrt{F_{obs}}-1.645)^{2}$.  Requiring the lower bound
to still give a $10\%$ Nagar relative bias,

$$\frac1{\mu^{2}_{L}}\le 0.10\iff\mu^{2}_{L}\ge10,
$$

gives

$$\sqrt{F^{*}}\ge\sqrt{10}+z_{0.95}, $$

i.e. on the $\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu^{2})$ scale

$$F^{*}_{0.95}\approx\bigl(\sqrt{10}+1.645\bigr)^{2}
      \approx(3.162+1.645)^{2}\approx 23.1\approx 23 ,
$$

so that $F_{obs}\gtrsim 23$ puts the $95\%$ one sided lower bound
$\mu^{2}_{L}$ at $\mu^{2}_{L}\ge10$ and hence 
${\rm RB}_{L}\approx\mu^{-2}_{L}\le0.10$.  With the usual $F=1+\mu^{2}$
normalisation this is $F^{*}\approx1+(\sqrt{10}+1.645)^{2}\approx24$,
the familiar $F\approx20\!-\!25$ $95\%$ lower confidence rule, which
collapses to the point Nagar rule $1/F\approx0.10$, $F\approx10$,
$F-1\approx11$, and to the Stock–Yogo finite sample $10\%$ maximal
relative bias critical value $F_{SY}\approx16.4$.  The $ \approx23$
number is the $95\%$ one-sided lower confidence bound on $\mu^{2}$,
$F\approx26$ on the conventional two-sided $z_{0.975}=1.96$ calibration.

For a just identified homoscedastic model the first order Nagar relative
bias is

$R(\mu^{2})\approx k\,\mu^{-2},\qquad k=1$,

and in large samples

$F_{1}\;\dot\sim\;\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu^{2}),\qquad 
\sqrt{F_{1}}=\sqrt{\mu^{2}}+Z+o_{p}(1),\;Z\sim N(0,1)$,
so that on the $\sqrt F$ scale

${\rm E}\sqrt{F_{1}}\approx\sqrt{\mu^{2}},\qquad {\rm Var}\sqrt{F_{1}}\approx 1 $.

Put $R_{0}=0.10$.  On the Nagar scale

$\mu_{0}^{2}=k/R_{0}=1/0.10=10,\qquad a_{0}=\sqrt{\mu_{0}^{2}}=\sqrt{10}$.

A one-sided $95\%$ lower confidence bound for $\sqrt{\mu^{2}}$ based on
the observed first stage $t_{1}=\sqrt{F_{1}}$ is

$\sqrt{\mu^{2}}_{L}=t_{1}-z_{0.95},\qquad z_{0.95}=1.645 .$

Requiring $\mu^{2}_{L}\ge\mu_{0}^{2}$,

$t_{1}^{*}\ge a_{0}+z_{0.95},\qquad 
t_{1}^{*}= \sqrt{10}+1.645\approx4.81,$

i.e. on the $\mu^{2}\approx F$ normalisation

$F_{0.95}^{*}\approx t_{1}^{*2}
       =\bigl(\sqrt{10}+1.645\bigr)^{2}\approx 23.1\approx23$ ,

so that $F_{1}\gtrsim 23\!-\!24$ puts the $95\%$ lower confidence bound
for the concentration parameter at $\mu^{2}\ge10$ and hence
$R(\mu^{2})\approx\mu^{-2}\le0.10$ with $95\%$ confidence.  On the
customary $E F_{1}=1+\mu^{2}$ normalisation $\mu^{2}=F_{1}-1$ and

$\sqrt{F_{1}-1}\ge\sqrt{10}+1.645\;\Longleftrightarrow\;
F_{1}\ge1+\bigl(\sqrt{10}+1.645\bigr)^{2}\approx24.1$,

the familiar $F\gtrsim22\!-\!25$ $95\%$ lower bound, the point Nagar
rule $R\approx1/F$ being $F_{0}\approx10$, $F_{0}-1\approx11$.
The two-sided $z_{0.975}=1.96$ version is
$F^{*}\approx(\sqrt{10}+1.96)^{2}\approx26.2$.  This is the $F>10$ rule
uprated to the usual $95\%$ confidence Stock–Yogo $10\%$ maximal
relative-bias value $F_{SY}\approx16.38\approx16\!-\!17$ on the
size–distortion scale. ∎

${\rm RB}_{N}\simeq\frac{k}{\mu^{2}},\qquad

so that on the population scale

${\rm RB}_{N}\simeq\mu^{-2}\simeq\frac{1}{F-1}\simeq\frac1F $

in large samples.  The usual $10\%$ point is therefore

$\mu_{0}^{2}=k/0.10=10$ ,   ${\rm E}F_{0}=1+\mu_{0}^{2}=11$,

the familiar $F\approx10$ rule.

$t_{1}=\sqrt{F_{1}}\;\dot\sim\;N\!\left(\sqrt{\mu^{2}},1\right)
$,
i.e. $F_{1}\dot\sim \chi^{2}_{1}(\mu^{2})=(Z+\sqrt{\mu^{2}})^{2}$.
Hence a one–sided $95\%$ lower confidence limit for $\sqrt{\mu^{2}}$
is

$\sqrt{\hat\mu^{2}_{L}}=\sqrt{F_{1}}-z_{0.95},\qquad
z_{0.95}=1.645,$

so that

$\widehat{{\rm RB}}_{U}\simeq \hat\mu_{L}^{-2}
      =\bigl(\sqrt{F_{1}}-z_{0.95}\bigr)^{-2}$.

Requiring $\widehat{{\rm RB}}_{U}\le0.10$, i.e. $\hat\mu_{L}^{2}\ge
\mu_{0}^{2}$, gives

$\sqrt{F_{1}^{*}}\ge \sqrt{\mu_{0}^{2}}+z_{0.95}$,

i.e. on the $\mu^{2}\approx F$ normalisation

$F_{1}^{*}\approx\Bigl(\sqrt{10}+1.645\Bigr)^{2}
      \approx\bigl(3.162+1.645\bigr)^{2}
      \approx 23.1\approx 23$

for a one–sided $95\%$ lower bound, $F_{1}^{*}\approx(\sqrt{10}
+1.96)^{2}\approx26$ on the two–sided $z_{0.975}$ version.  In the
conventional $E F=1+\mu^{2}$ normalisation this is
$F_{1}^{*}\approx1+(\sqrt{10}+1.645)^{2}\approx24\!-\!25$,
essentially $F_{1}\gtrsim22\!-\!24$, the textbook $F>10$ rule
inflated by the $z_{0.95}$ sampling correction.

$F_{SY}(1,1;{\rm rel.~bias}=0.10)\approx16.38\approx16\!-\!17$,

approximation $F\approx16.4$ Stock–Yogo value quoted above. ∎

The Nagar first-order homoscedastic relative 2SLS-to-OLS bias for one endogenous regressor and one instrument is 
$R\simeq k/\mu^{2}$ with $k=1$, so $R\simeq\mu^{-2}\simeq (E F-1)^{-1}\simeq F^{-1}$ in large samples. The point $10\%$ rule is $1/F\approx0.10\iff F\approx10$, $F-1\approx10\iff F\approx11$, the Staiger-Stock $F>10$ rule of thumb.

In the weak-instrument limit $kF\to\chi_{k}^{2}(\mu^{2})$ and for $k=1$
$\sqrt F =\sqrt{\mu^{2}}+Z+o_{p}(1)$, $Z\sim N(0,1)$, i.e. $\sqrt F\approx N(\sqrt{\mu^{2}},1)$.
A one-sided $95\%$ lower confidence bound for $\sqrt{\mu^{2}}$ is 
$\sqrt{\mu^{2}_{L}}=\sqrt F-z_{0.95}$ with $z_{0.95}=1.645$, so
$\mu^{2}_{L}=(\sqrt F-1.645)^{2}$.

Requiring the lower bound to still imply a $10\%$ Nagar bias,
$\mu^{2}_{L}\ge\mu^{2}_{0}$ with $\mu^{2}_{0}=1/0.10=10$, gives
$\sqrt{F^{*}}\ge\sqrt{10}+1.645$. On the $\mu^{2}\approx F$ normalisation
$F^{*}=(\sqrt{10}+1.645)^{2}\approx4.81^{2}\approx23.1\approx23\!-\!24$,
about $F^{*}\approx24.1$ on the conventional $E F=1+\mu^{2}$, i.e. $\mu^{2}=F-1$, 
normalisation $\sqrt{F-1}\ge\sqrt{10}+1.645$.
With the two-sided $z_{0.975}=1.96$ this is $(\sqrt{10}+1.96)^{2}\approx26.2$.
The point Nagar rule collapses to $F_{0}\approx10$, $F_{0}-1\approx11$.

This is distinct from the operational Stock-Yogo finite-sample inversion.
Using the delta method on $r=1/F$, ${\rm sd}(r)\simeq\sqrt2/F^{3/2}$,
$r_{U}=1/F+z_{0.95}\sqrt2/F^{3/2}<0.10$ gives $F\approx15\!-\!20$, and the
Stock-Yogo $5\%$ size maximal-relative-bias table for $k_{2}=1,L=1$ is
$F_{SY}(10\%\,\text{rel bias})\approx16.38\approx16\!-\!17$, the $F>10$ rule
inflated for sampling uncertainty. Colleagues 7,10,13,14 emphasize this
$16\!-\!17$ operational value, while Colleagues 1,3,4,6,8,11,12,15 give the
strict $95\%$ lower-confidence bound for $\mu^{2}$ itself,
$F\approx23\!-\!24$, $F\approx22\!-\!26$ depending on the $+1$ shift and
one- vs two-sided $z$.

Unresolved normalisation: $\mu^{2}\approx F$ vs $\mu^{2}\approx F-1$ moves
the point rule $10\to11$ and the $95\%$ bound $23.1\to24.1$. The conventional
textbook $F>10$ is the mean-bias point; the conservative Nagar $95\%$ lower
confidence bound for $\mu^{2}$ is $\approx23$ on the $\chi^{2}_{1}$ scale,
$\approx24$ on the $F=1+\mu^{2}$ scale; the Stock-Yogo size-distortion
calibration most often quoted in practice is $F\approx16\!-\!17$.
Current belief is the strict confidence bound is $\approx23$, essentially $23\!-\!24$,
with the operational Stock-Yogo value $\approx16$ being the commonly quoted
finite-sample rule.

distortion inversion of the same first order Nagar bias is the
conventional $5\%$ size $10\%$ maximal relative bias critical value
$F_{SY}(k_{2}=1,L=1)=16.38\approx16\!-\!17$, i.e. the $F>10$ point
Nagar rule inflated to $F\gtrsim16$ in finite sample use. ∎

12.text:
For a just identified homoskedastic model

${\rm RB}_{N}\equiv 
\frac{{\rm E}[\hat\beta_{2SLS}-\beta]}{{\rm E}[\hat\beta_{OLS}-\beta]}
\approx\frac{k}{\mu^{2}}\approx\frac1{\mu^{2}}, \qquad k=1 ,
$

and in the weak instrument limit

$kF_{1}\xrightarrow{d}\chi^{2}_{k}(\mu^{2}),\qquad 
\sqrt{F_{1}}=\sqrt{\mu^{2}}+Z+o_{p}(1),\; Z\sim N(0,1)$

so that on the $\sqrt F$ scale

${\rm E}\sqrt{F_{1}}\approx\sqrt{\mu^{2}},\qquad 
{\rm sd}\sqrt{F_{1}}\approx1 $ .

Hence a one–sided $95\%$ normal lower confidence bound for the
concentration parameter is

$\sqrt{\hat\mu^{2}_{L}}=\sqrt{F_{obs}}-z_{0.95}, \qquad 
z_{0.95}=1.645,
$

i.e. $\hat\mu^{2}_{L}=(\sqrt{F_{obs}}-1.645)^{2}$ on the
$\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu^{2})$ normalisation. On the Nagar scale

${\rm RB}_{U}\approx \hat\mu_{L}^{-2}
      =\bigl(\sqrt{F_{obs}}-z_{0.95}\bigr)^{-2}.$

The $10\%$ Nagar point is

${\rm RB}_{0}=0.10\iff \mu^{2}_{0}=k/0.10=10,\qquad 
\sqrt{\mu^{2}_{0}}=\sqrt{10}\simeq3.162,
$

${\rm E}F_{0}=1+\mu^{2}_{0}\simeq11$, the textbook $1/F\approx0.10$
rule $F_{0}\approx10$, $F_{0}-1\approx11$.

Requiring the $95\%$ lower bound to still be at the $10\%$ bias
point,

$\hat\mu^{2}_{L}\ge\mu^{2}_{0}\iff 
\sqrt{F^{*}}\ge\sqrt{\mu^{2}_{0}}+z_{0.95},$

i.e.

$\sqrt{F^{*}}=\sqrt{10}+1.645\approx3.162+1.645\approx4.807,$

so that on the $\mu^{2}\approx F$, i.e. $\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu^{2})$, 
normalisation

$F^{*}_{0.95}\approx\bigl(\sqrt{10}+1.645\bigr)^{2}
       \approx4.81^{2}\approx23.1\approx23$

gives $ \mu^{2}_{L}=(\sqrt{F^{*}}-1.645)^{2}\ge10$ and hence
${\rm RB}_{L}\approx1/\mu^{2}_{L}\le0.10$ with one-sided $95\%$
confidence.  On the conventional $E F=1+\mu^{2}$, $\mu^{2}=F-1$
normalisation this is $\sqrt{F^{*}-1}\ge\sqrt{10}+1.645$,
$F^{*}\approx1+(\sqrt{10}+1.645)^{2}\approx24.1\approx24$, i.e.
$F\gtrsim22\!-\!25$ for a genuine $95\%$ lower confidence bound
$\mu^{2}>10$.  The two-sided $z_{0.975}=1.96$ version is
$(\sqrt{10}+1.96)^{2}\approx26.2$.

This is the $F>10$ point Nagar rule $R\approx1/F$ inflated by the
$z_{0.95}$ sampling error in $\sqrt F$.  The finite-sample Stock–Yogo
inversion of the same Nagar approximation, the $5\%$ size $10\%$
maximal relative-bias critical value, is the operationally quoted

$F_{SY}(k_{2}=1,L=1;{\rm rel.\,bias}=0.10)\approx16.38\approx16\!-\!17,$

i.e. the familiar $F\gtrsim16$ weak-instrument rule, $F\approx10$ on a
point mean basis. ∎

1.text:
For the homoskedastic just identified case the Nagar first order mean
relative bias is

${\rm RB}(\mu^{2})=\frac{{\rm E}[\hat\beta_{2SLS}-\beta]}
{{\rm E}[\hat\beta_{OLS}-\beta]}\approx \frac{k}{\mu^{2}}$,
$k=1$,

i.e. on the population scale 
${\rm RB}\approx\mu^{-2}\approx (F-1)^{-1}\approx F^{-1}$ .
On the weak instrument scale  

$kF\;\dot\sim \;\chi_{k}^{2}(\mu^{2})$  and for $k=1$ up to $o_{p}(1)$

$\sqrt F =\sqrt{\mu^{2}}+Z,\qquad Z\sim N(0,1)$,

so that on the $\sqrt F$ scale

${\rm E}\sqrt F \approx\sqrt{\mu^{2}},\qquad {\rm sd}\sqrt F\approx1$.
A one sided $95\%$ normal lower bound for $\sqrt{\mu^{2}}$ is therefore

$\sqrt{\hat\mu_{L}^{2}}=\sqrt{F_{obs}}-z_{0.95}$,
$z_{0.95}=1.645$,

i.e. $\hat\mu_{L}^{2}=(\sqrt{F_{obs}}-1.645)^{2}$ on the
$\chi_{1}^{2}(\mu^{2})$ scale.  The point Nagar $10\%$ bias is

$\mu_{0}^{2}=k/0.10=10$, $\sqrt{\mu_{0}^{2}}=\sqrt{10}\approx3.16$.

Requiring the $95\%$ lower bound to still be at the $10\%$ Nagar point,

$\hat\mu_{L}^{2}\ge\mu_{0}^{2}\iff 
\sqrt{F^{*}}\ge\sqrt{\mu_{0}^{2}}+z_{0.95}$,

gives on the $\mu^{2}\approx F$ normalisation

$\sqrt{F^{*}}=\sqrt{10}+1.645\approx3.162+1.645\approx4.81$,

$\displaystyle 
F_{0.95}^{*}\approx\bigl(\sqrt{10}+1.645\bigr)^{2}\approx 23.1\approx23$,
i.e. $F_{obs}\gtrsim 22\!-\!24$ puts the one sided $95\%$ lower
confidence bound $\mu_{L}^{2}=(\sqrt F-1.645)^{2}$ at $\mu_{L}^{2}\ge10$
and hence ${\rm RB}_{L}\approx\mu_{L}^{-2}\le0.10$ with $95\%$ one sided
confidence.  On the conventional $E F=1+\mu^{2}$,
${\rm RB}\approx(F-1)^{-1}$ normalisation this is
$\sqrt{F^{*}-1}\ge\sqrt{10}+1.645$,
$F^{*}\approx1+(\sqrt{10}+1.645)^{2}\approx24.1$, the familiar $F\approx
22\!-\!26$ $95\%$ lower confidence inflation of the point Nagar rule
${\rm RB}\approx1/F$, $F_{0}\approx1/0.10=10$, $F_{0}-1\approx11$.
With the $z_{0.975}=1.96$ two sided calibration this is
$(\sqrt{10}+1.96)^{2}\approx26$.  The point Nagar rule is the
textbook $F>10$ rule, $F\approx16.4$ being the Stock–Yogo $5\%$ size
$10\%$ maximal relative bias finite sample inversion of the same
approximation.

2.text:
For a just identified homoscedastic first stage with $L=1$

${\rm RB}_{N}:=\frac{E\hat\beta_{2SLS}-\beta}{E\hat\beta_{OLS}-\beta}
     \simeq \frac{L}{\mu^{2}}\simeq\frac1{\mu^{2}}\simeq\frac{1}{F-1}
     \simeq\frac1F $

and in the weak instrument limit

$kF\;\dot \sim\;\chi_{k}^{2}(\mu^{2})$ , $k=1$,

so that up to $o_{p}(1)$

$t_{1}:=\sqrt{F_{1}}=\sqrt{\mu^{2}}+Z$, $Z\sim N(0,1)$,
${\rm E}F_{1}=1+\mu^{2}$.

On the Nagar scale $R_{0}=0.10$ is

$\mu_{0}^{2}=L/R_{0}=10$, $\sqrt{\mu_{0}^{2}}=\sqrt{10}\approx3.162$,

and 
${\rm E}F_{0}=1+\mu_{0}^{2}\approx 11$, the familiar $1/F\approx0.10$
point $F_{0}\approx10$ rule.  A one sided $95\%$ normal lower bound for
$\sqrt{\mu^{2}}$ is

$\sqrt{\hat\mu^{2}_{L}}=\sqrt{F_{1}}-z_{0.95}$,  $z_{0.95}=1.645$,

i.e. $\hat\mu^{2}_{L}=(\sqrt{F_{1}}-1.645)^{2}$ on the $\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu^{2})$
scale and ${\rm RB}_{U}\simeq\hat\mu_{L}^{-2}$.  Requiring the $95\%$ lower
bound to still be a $10\%$ Nagar relative bias,

$\hat\mu^{2}_{L}\ge \mu_{0}^{2}$,

$\sqrt{F^{*}}\ge \sqrt{\mu_{0}^{2}}+z_{0.95}$,

so that on the $\mu^{2}\approx F$ normalisation

$\sqrt{F^{*}}\ge \sqrt{10}+1.645\approx4.81$,

$F^{*}_{0.95}\approx\bigl(\sqrt{10}+1.645\bigr)^{2}\approx 23.1\approx
22\!-\!24$,

i.e. $F_{1}\gtrsim23$ puts $\mu^{2}_{L}=(\sqrt{F_{1}}-1.645)^{2}\ge10$ and
hence $R_{L}\simeq\mu_{L}^{-2}\le0.10$ with $95\%$ one-sided confidence.
On the conventional $E F=1+\mu^{2}$, $\mu^{2}=F-1$, normalisation this is

$\sqrt{F^{*}-1}\ge\sqrt{10}+1.645$,

$F^{*}\approx1+(\sqrt{10}+1.645)^{2}\approx24.1\approx24$,

the familiar $F\approx20\!-\!25$ $95\%$ lower confidence inflation of the
point Nagar $F_{0}\approx10$, $F_{0}-1\approx11$, rule.  With the usual
two-sided $z_{0.975}=1.96$ this is $F^{*}\approx(\sqrt{10}+1.96)^{2}\approx
26$.

In particular the point Nagar rule is $R\approx1/F$, $F_{0}\approx1/0.10
=10$, $E F_{0}=11$.  Inverted on the finite sample Stock–Yogo maximal
relative-bias $5\%$ size scale the same Nagar first order approximation
gives the operationally quoted

$F_{SY}(k_{2}=1,L=1;{\rm rel.\,bias}=0.10)\approx16.38\approx16\!-\!17$,

i.e. the $F>10$ point rule inflated to $F\gtrsim16$ in finite sample
practice, the $23\!-\!24$ number above being the strict $95\%$ one-sided
lower confidence bound for $\mu^{2}$ itself. ∎

6.text:
For a just identified homoskedastic model

${\rm RB}_{N}\approx\frac{k}{\mu^{2}}\approx \frac{1}{\mu^{2}}$ , 
$k=1$,

and in the weak instrument limit

$kF\;\xrightarrow d\; \chi^{2}_{k}(\mu^{2})$ , 

so that up to $o_{p}(1)$

$\sqrt F =\sqrt{\mu^{2}}+Z$,  $Z\sim N(0,1)$ ,    i.e. 
${\rm E}\sqrt F\approx\sqrt{\mu^{2}}$, ${\rm Var}\sqrt F\approx1$.

The point Nagar $10\%$ rule is

$R_{0}=0.10\iff\mu_{0}^{2}=k/R_{0}=10$,      $\sqrt{\mu_{0}^{2}}=\sqrt{10}\approx3.16$,

${\rm E}F_{0}=1+\mu_{0}^{2}\approx11$ , the familiar $F\approx10$ rule
$R\approx1/F$.

A one sided $95\%$ normal lower bound for $\sqrt{\mu^{2}}$ is

$\sqrt{\mu^{2}_{L}}=\sqrt{F_{obs}}-z_{0.95}$,  $z_{0.95}=1.645$,

i.e.  $\mu^{2}_{L}= \bigl(\sqrt{F_{obs}}-1.645\bigr)^{2}$.
Requiring the lower bound to still deliver the $10\%$ Nagar bias,

$\mu^{2}_{L}\ge\mu_{0}^{2}=10$,

$\sqrt{F^{*}}\ge\sqrt{\mu_{0}^{2}}+z_{0.95}$,

so that on the $\mu^{2}\approx F$ $\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu^{2})$ normalisation

$F^{*}_{0.95}\approx\Bigl(\sqrt{10}+1.645\Bigr)^{2}
       \approx(3.162+1.645)^{2}\approx23.1\approx23$,

i.e. $F_{obs}\gtrsim22\!-\!24$ puts $\mu^{2}_{L}=(\sqrt F-1.645)^{2}\ge10$
and hence $R_{L}\approx\mu_{L}^{-2}\le0.10$ with one-sided $95\%$
confidence.  With the conventional $ {\rm E}F=1+\mu^{2}$, $\mu^{2}=F-1$,
normalisation

$\sqrt{F^{*}-1}\ge\sqrt{10}+1.645$,

$F^{*}-1\approx23.1$, $F^{*}\approx24.1\approx24$, the familiar
$F\approx 22\!-\!26$ $95\%$ lower confidence inflation of the point
$F\approx10$, $F-1\approx11$ Nagar rule.  Two sided $z_{0.975}=1.96$
gives $(\sqrt{10}+1.96)^{2}\approx26.2$.

In particular the point Nagar rule is $R\approx1/F$, $F_{0}\approx
1/0.10=10$.  The finite-sample Stock–Yogo $5\%$ size inversion of the
same Nagar first order bias is the operationally quoted

$F_{SY}(k_{2}=1,L=1;{\rm rel.\,bias}=0.10)\approx16.38\approx16\!-\!17$,

the $F>10$ point rule inflated for sampling uncertainty, which is the
$F\gtrsim16$ weak-instrument rule normally used in practice. ∎

11.text:
With one instrument the homoscedastic Nagar first order relative bias is

${\rm RB}(\mu^{2})\approx \frac{k}{\mu^{2}},\qquad k=1,$

${\rm RB}\approx\mu^{-2}\approx (F-1)^{-1}\approx F^{-1}$,

in the weak instrument limit

$kF\;\xrightarrow{d}\;\chi_{k}^{2}(\mu^{2}),\qquad 
\sqrt{F}= \sqrt{\mu^{2}}+Z+o_{p}(1),\;Z\sim N(0,1),$

so that on the $\sqrt F$ scale

${\rm E}\sqrt F\approx\sqrt{\mu^{2}},\qquad {\rm Var}\sqrt F\approx1.$

Put $R_{0}=0.10$. On the Nagar scale

$\mu_{0}^{2}=k/R_{0}=10,\qquad \sqrt{\mu_{0}^{2}}=\sqrt{10}\approx3.16$,

and on the mean scale $ {\rm E}F=1+\mu^{2}$ the point Nagar rule is
$R\approx1/F$, $F_{0}\approx1/R_{0}\approx10$, $E F_{0}\approx11$.

A one-sided $95\%$ normal lower confidence bound for $\sqrt{\mu^{2}}$ is

$\sqrt{\hat\mu_{L}^{2}}=\sqrt{F_{obs}}-z_{0.95},\qquad z_{0.95}=1.645,$

i.e. $\hat\mu_{L}^{2}=(\sqrt{F_{obs}}-1.645)^{2}$ on the $\chi_{1}^{2}(\mu^{2})$
normalisation.  Requiring the $95\%$ lower bound to still be the $10\%$
Nagar bias, $\hat\mu_{L}^{2}\ge\mu_{0}^{2}$,

$\sqrt{F^{*}}\ge\sqrt{\mu_{0}^{2}}+z_{0.95},$

i.e. on the $\mu^{2}\approx F$ normalisation

$F^{*}\approx\Bigl(\sqrt{10}+1.645\Bigr)^{2}
      \approx(3.162+1.645)^{2}
      \approx4.81^{2}\approx23.1\approx23,$

so that $\mu_{L}^{2}=(\sqrt F-1.645)^{2}>10$ and
${\rm RB}_{L}\approx\mu_{L}^{-2}<0.10$ with one-sided $95\%$ confidence.
On the conventional $E F=1+\mu^{2}$, $\mu^{2}=F-1$, normalisation this is

$\sqrt{F^{*}-1}\ge\sqrt{10}+1.645\iff 
F^{*}\approx1+\bigl(\sqrt{10}+1.645\bigr)^{2}\approx24.1\approx24,$

the familiar $F\approx22$–$25$ $95\%$ lower confidence inflation of the
point Nagar $F\approx10$, $F-1\approx11$, Staiger-Stock rule.  With the
two-sided $z_{0.975}=1.96$ calibration $F^{*}\approx(\sqrt{10}+1.96)^{2}
\approx26$.

In particular the point Nagar rule is $R\approx1/F$, $F_{0}\approx10$.
Inverting the non-central $F$ on the Stock–Yogo maximal relative bias
scale the $5\%$ size $10\%$ maximal relative bias critical value is the
operationally quoted

$F_{SY}(k_{2}=1,L=1;{\rm rel\,bias}=0.10)\approx16.38\approx16\!-\!17,$

i.e. the $F>10$ point rule inflated to the usual $F\gtrsim16$ weak
instrument rule.  This is the $23\!-\!24$ formal $\mu^{2}_{L}$ lower
confidence bound, $F\approx16.4$ on the usual Stock–Yogo size-distortion
calibration.

8.text:
For the just identified homoskedastic model

${\rm RB}_{N}\simeq\frac{k}{\mu^{2}},\qquad k=1$,

${\rm RB}_{N}\simeq\mu^{-2}\simeq (F-1)^{-1}\simeq F^{-1}$
in large samples and

$kF\;\dot\sim\;\chi^{2}_{k}(\mu^{2})$,  $E F =1+\mu^{2}/k$ .
In particular with $k=1$,

$F\dot\sim\bigl(Z+\sqrt{\mu^{2}}\bigr)^{2}, \qquad 
\sqrt F=\sqrt{\mu^{2}}+Z+o_{p}(1),\; Z\sim N(0,1)$

so that on the $\sqrt F$ scale

${\rm sd}\bigl(\sqrt F\bigr)\approx 1$ .

Put $R_{0}=0.10$.  On the Nagar scale

$\mu_{0}^{2}=k/R_{0}=10,\qquad a_{0}=\sqrt{\mu_{0}^{2}}=\sqrt{10}\approx3.16$,

and the point Nagar $10\%$ rule is $R_{0}\approx1/\mu_{0}^{2}\approx
1/F_{0}$ i.e. $F_{0}\approx10$, $E F_{0}=1+\mu_{0}^{2}\approx11$,
the familiar $F>10$ Staiger–Stock rule.

A one sided $95\%$ normal lower bound for $\sqrt{\mu^{2}}$ is

$\sqrt{\mu^{2}_{L}}=\sqrt F-z_{0.95},\qquad z_{0.95}=1.645,$

i.e. $\mu^{2}_{L}=(\sqrt F-1.645)^{2}$ on the $\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu^{2})$
scale.  Requiring the lower bound to still give a $10\%$ Nagar
relative bias,

$\mu^{2}_{L}\ge\mu_{0}^{2}$,

$\sqrt{F^{*}}\ge\sqrt{\mu_{0}^{2}}+z_{0.95}$,

i.e.

$\sqrt{F^{*}}=\sqrt{10}+1.645\approx3.162+1.645\approx4.81$,

$F^{*}_{\chi^{2}}\approx\bigl(\sqrt{10}+1.645\bigr)^{2}\approx23.1$,
$F^{*}\approx22\!-\!24$, the $95\%$ one sided lower confidence bound for
the concentration parameter.  On the conventional $E F=1+\mu^{2}$,
$\mu^{2}=F-1$, normalisation this is

$\sqrt{F^{*}-1}\ge\sqrt{10}+1.645$,

$F^{*}\approx1+\bigl(\sqrt{10}+1.645\bigr)^{2}\approx24.1\approx24$,
essentially $F\gtrsim20\!-\!25$ for a genuine $95\%$ lower bound
$\mu^{2}_{L}\ge10\iff R_{L}\approx\mu^{-2}_{L}\le0.10$.  With the usual
two sided $z_{0.975}=1.96$ this is $(\sqrt{10}+1.96)^{2}\approx26.2$.

Neglecting the $+1$ shift this is the textbook $R\approx1/F$ point
$F_{0}\approx1/0.10=10$, $F_{0}-1\approx11$.  Inverting the non-central
$F$ law on the Stock–Yogo maximal-relative-bias $5\%$ size scale the
finite-sample operational critical value is

$F_{SY}(k_{2}=1,L=1;{\rm rel.\,bias}=0.10)\approx16.38\approx16\!-\!17$,

i.e. the familiar $F>10$ point rule inflated for sampling uncertainty
to the $F\gtrsim16$ weak-instrument rule that is quoted in practice.

3.text:
For a just identified homoscedastic model with $L=1$ the Nagar first order
relative bias is

${\rm RB}(\mu^{2})=\frac{{\rm plim}\;\hat\beta_{2SLS}-\beta}
{{\rm plim}\;\hat\beta_{OLS}-\beta}\simeq \frac{L}{\mu^{2}}
\simeq\frac1{\mu^{2}}$

and in the weak instrument limit

$kF\;\xrightarrow{d}\;\chi^{2}_{k}(\mu^{2})$, $k=1$,

so that up to $o_{p}(1)$

$\sqrt{F}= \sqrt{\mu^{2}}+Z,\qquad Z\sim N(0,1),$

and ${\rm E}F=1+\mu^{2}$.  On the mean scale

${\rm RB}_{0}=0.10\iff \mu^{2}_{0}=L/0.10=10$,

${\rm E}F_{0}=1+\mu^{2}_{0}\simeq 11$, the familiar $F\approx10$ Staiger-Stock
point rule $ {\rm RB}\approx1/F$.

Put $t=\sqrt{F}$.  A one sided $95\%$ normal lower confidence bound for
$\sqrt{\mu^{2}}$ is

$\sqrt{\hat\mu^{2}_{L}}=t-z_{0.95},\qquad z_{0.95}=1.645,$

i.e. $\hat\mu^{2}_{L}=(\sqrt F-z_{0.95})^{2}$ on the $\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu^{2})$
scale.  Requiring

${\rm RB}_{U}\simeq \hat\mu_{L}^{-2}\le 0.10\iff \hat\mu_{L}^{2}\ge\mu^{2}_{0}=10$

gives

$\sqrt{F^{*}}\ge\sqrt{\mu^{2}_{0}}+z_{0.95}$,

$\sqrt{F^{*}}\ge\sqrt{10}+1.645\approx3.162+1.645=4.81,$

i.e. on the $\mu^{2}\approx F$ normalisation

$F^{*}\approx\bigl(\sqrt{10}+1.645\bigr)^{2}\approx 23.1\approx 23$

for the $95\%$ one-sided lower confidence bound $\mu^{2}_{L}\ge10$.
On the conventional ${\rm E}F=1+\mu^{2}$, $\mu^{2}=F-1$ normalisation this is

$\sqrt{F^{*}-1}\ge\sqrt{10}+1.645\;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\;
F^{*}\approx1+\bigl(\sqrt{10}+1.645\bigr)^{2}\approx24.1\approx24,$

$F\gtrsim22$–$25$ in round numbers, the $F\approx10$ point Nagar rule
up-rated by the $z_{0.95}$ sampling error in $\sqrt F$.
The two–sided $z_{0.975}=1.96$ version is
$F^{*}\approx(\sqrt{10}+1.96)^{2}\approx26$.

In the usual Stock–Yogo finite-sample inversion of the same Nagar
first order bias the $5\%$ size $10\%$ maximal relative bias critical
value is the operationally quoted

$F_{SY}(k_{2}=1,L=1;0.10)\approx16.38\approx16\!-\!17$,

i.e. the $F\approx10$ point rule inflated to the familiar $F\gtrsim16$
weak-instrument rule, the $23\!-\!24$ number above being the strict
$95\%$ lower-confidence bound for the concentration parameter
$\mu^{2}_{L}=(\sqrt F-1.645)^{2}>10$. ∎

5.text:
For a just identified homoskedastic model

${\rm RB}_{N}\simeq {\rm E}\hat\beta_{2SLS}-\beta\big/
{\rm E}\hat\beta_{OLS}-\beta\simeq k\mu^{-2}$,
$k=1$ , so that on the population scale

${\rm RB}_{N}\simeq\mu^{-2}\simeq (F-1)^{-1}\simeq F^{-1}$,
 ${\rm E}F=1+\mu^{2}$ .

On the weak instrument scale $kF\to_{d}\chi_{k}^{2}(\mu^{2})$ and for
$k=1$ up to $o_{p}(1)$

$F\approx\bigl(Z+\sqrt{\mu^{2}}\bigr)^{2},\qquad Z\sim N(0,1),$

i.e.

$\sqrt{F}= \sqrt{\mu^{2}}+Z+o_{p}(1)$,
${\rm E}\sqrt{F}\approx\sqrt{\mu^{2}}$, ${\rm Var}\sqrt{F}\approx1$.

Hence a one sided 95$\%$ normal lower confidence bound for
$\sqrt{\mu^{2}}$ based on the observed first stage $t=\sqrt{F}$ is

$\sqrt{\hat\mu_{L}^{2}}=t-z_{0.95},\qquad z_{0.95}=1.645,$
$\hat\mu_{L}^{2}=( \sqrt{F}-1.645)^{2}$.

The Nagar 10$\%$ point is

${\rm RB}_{0}=0.10\iff\mu_{0}^{2}=k/0.10=10$,
$\sqrt{\mu_{0}^{2}}=\sqrt{10}\approx3.162$.

Requiring the 95$\%$ lower bound to still be at the 10$\%$ bias point,

$\hat\mu_{L}^{2}\ge\mu_{0}^{2}\iff 
\sqrt{F}\ge\sqrt{\mu_{0}^{2}}+z_{0.95}$,

i.e. on the $\mu^{2}\approx F$ $\chi_{1}^{2}(\mu^{2})$ normalisation

$F_{0.95}^{*}= \bigl(\sqrt{10}+1.645\bigr)^{2}
           \approx(3.162+1.645)^{2}\approx4.81^{2}\approx23.1$,

so that $F\gtrsim23$–$24$ puts the one-sided 95$\%$ lower bound
$\mu_{L}^{2}=(\sqrt{F}-1.645)^{2}$ at $\mu_{L}^{2}\ge10$ and hence
${\rm RB}_{L}\approx\mu_{L}^{-2}\le0.10$ with 95$\%$ confidence.
On the conventional $E F=1+\mu^{2}$, $\mu^{2}=F-1$, normalisation

$\sqrt{F-1}\ge\sqrt{10}+1.645$

i.e.

$F_{0.95}^{*}\approx1+\bigl(\sqrt{10}+1.645\bigr)^{2}
        \approx24.1$,

the familiar $F\approx22$–$26$ $95\%$ lower-confidence inflation of
the point Nagar rule ${\rm RB}\approx1/F$, $F_{0}\approx1/0.10=10$,
$F_{0}-1\approx11$.  With the usual two-sided $z_{0.975}=1.96$ this is
$(\sqrt{10}+1.96)^{2}\approx26.2$.

In particular the point Nagar rule is $F\gtrsim10$, $F-1\gtrsim11$.
The finite-sample Stock–Yogo $5\%$ size inversion of the same Nagar
first order bias is the operationally quoted

$F_{SY}(k_{2}=1,L=1;{\rm rel.\,bias}=0.10)\approx16.38\approx16\!-\!17$,

i.e. the textbook $F>10$ rule inflated to $F\gtrsim16$ in practice,
the conventional $95\%$ confidence / $5\%$ size maximal-relative-bias
threshold.  This is the $\approx23$ normal mean$+1.64\,{\rm sd}$ bound
$F\approx23$ on the $\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu^{2})$ scale, $\approx24$ on the
$E F=1+\mu^{2}$ scale, often quoted as the $F\approx16$ Stock–Yogo rule.

10.text:
With one endogenous regressor and one instrument the homoscedastic first
order Nagar relative bias is

${\rm plim}\hat\beta_{2SLS}-\beta\simeq 
\frac{\sigma_{uv}}{\sigma_{v}^{2}}\frac1{\mu^{2}},\qquad
{\rm plim}\hat\beta_{OLS}-\beta=\frac{\sigma_{uv}}{\sigma_{v}^{2}}$

so that on the population scale

$R(\mu^{2}):=\frac{{\rm bias}_{2SLS}}{{\rm bias}_{OLS}}\simeq
\frac{1}{\mu^{2}},\qquad k=1,$

and in the weak instrument limit

$kF\;\dot\sim\;\chi^{2}_{k}\!\left(\mu^{2}\right),\qquad 
\sqrt F=\sqrt{\mu^{2}}+Z+o_{p}(1),\;Z\sim N(0,1),$

i.e. up to $o_{p}(1)$

$t_{1}=\sqrt{F_{1}}\approx N\!\left(\sqrt{\mu^{2}},1\right)$ .

Hence a one sided $95\%$ lower confidence bound for the non-centrality
is

$\sqrt{\mu^{2}_{L}}=\sqrt{F_{obs}}-z_{0.95},\qquad
z_{0.95}=1.645,$

$\mu^{2}_{L}=\bigl(\sqrt{F_{obs}}-1.645\bigr)^{2}$,

and on the Nagar scale

${\rm RB}_{U}\simeq\mu_{L}^{-2}=\bigl(\sqrt{F_{obs}}-1.645\bigr)^{-2}$.

The point Nagar $10\%$ rule is

$R_{0}=0.10\iff\mu_{0}^{2}=1/R_{0}=10,\qquad
\sqrt{\mu_{0}^{2}}=\sqrt{10}\approx3.16,$

$E F_{0}=1+\mu_{0}^{2}\approx11$, the familiar $F\approx10$ rule.
Requiring the $95\%$ lower bound to still be at the $10\%$ Nagar level,

$\mu^{2}_{L}\ge\mu_{0}^{2}\iff
\sqrt{F^{*}}\ge\sqrt{\mu_{0}^{2}}+z_{0.95},$

gives on the $\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu^{2})$ scale $\mu^{2}\approx F$

$\sqrt{F^{*}}\ge\sqrt{10}+1.645\approx3.162+1.645=4.81,$

$F_{0.95}^{*}\approx\bigl(\sqrt{10}+1.645\bigr)^{2}\approx23.1\approx23$,

so that $F_{1}\gtrsim23\!-\!24$ puts

$\mu^{2}_{L}=\bigl(\sqrt{F_{1}}-1.645\bigr)^{2}\ge10$,

i.e. ${\rm RB}_{U}\simeq\mu_{L}^{-2}\le0.10$ with one sided $95\%$
confidence.  On the conventional $E F=1+\mu^{2}$, $\mu^{2}=F-1$, 
normalisation this is $\sqrt{F^{*}-1}\ge\sqrt{10}+1.645$, i.e.

$F^{*}\approx1+\bigl(\sqrt{10}+1.645\bigr)^{2}\approx24.1$,

about $F\approx22\!-\!25$ for a genuine $95\%$ lower confidence bound
for $\mu^{2}$, $F\approx26$ on the two sided $z_{0.975}=1.96$ version.
Neglecting the $+1$ shift this is the $F\approx23$ $95\%$ lower confidence
inflation of the point Nagar $F_{0}\approx1/0.10\approx10$ rule,
commonly quoted as $F\gtrsim23\!-\!24$, $\approx24$ with the $F-1$
mapping.  The finite-sample Stock–Yogo $5\%$ size maximal-relative-bias
inversion of the same Nagar approximation is the operationally quoted
$F_{SY}(1,1;10\%)\approx16.38\approx16\!-\!17$, the $F>10$ point rule
inflated for sampling uncertainty.

9.text:
For a just identified homoskedastic first stage

${\rm RB}_{N}:=\frac{{\rm E}\hat\beta_{2SLS}-\beta}
               {{\rm E}\hat\beta_{OLS}-\beta}\approx\frac{k}{\mu^{2}}$,
$k=1$ , and on the weak instrument limit

$kF\;\xrightarrow{d}\;\chi^{2}_{k}(\mu^{2}),\qquad 
\sqrt F=\sqrt{\mu^{2}}+Z+o_{p}(1),\;Z\sim N(0,1)$,

so that up to $o_{p}(1)$

${\rm E}\sqrt F\approx\sqrt{\mu^{2}},\qquad 
{\rm sd}\sqrt F\approx1$.
On the Nagar scale ${\rm RB}_{N}\approx\mu^{-2}$.

On the point Nagar scale

${\rm RB}_{N}=0.10\iff \mu_{0}^{2}=k/0.10=10$,

${\rm E}F_{0}=1+\mu_{0}^{2}=11$, i.e. the familiar $1/F\approx0.10$
point rule $F_{0}\approx10$, $F_{0}-1\approx11$.

A one-sided $95\%$ normal lower bound for $\sqrt{\mu^{2}}$ based on the
observed first stage $t_{1}=\sqrt F$ is

$\sqrt{\hat\mu_{L}^{2}}=\sqrt F-z_{0.95},\qquad z_{0.95}=1.645,$

i.e. $\hat\mu_{L}^{2}=(\sqrt F-1.645)^{2}$ on the $\chi_{1}^{2}(\mu^{2})$
scale.  On the Nagar scale the $95\%$ upper bound for the relative
bias is ${\rm RB}_{U}\approx\hat\mu_{L}^{-2}$.  Requiring
${\rm RB}_{U}\le0.10$, i.e. $\hat\mu_{L}^{2}\ge\mu_{0}^{2}=10$, is

$\sqrt{F^{*}}\ge\sqrt{\mu_{0}^{2}}+z_{0.95}$,
$\sqrt{F^{*}}\ge\sqrt{10}+1.645\approx3.162+1.645=4.81$,

i.e. on the $\mu^{2}\approx F$ normalisation

$F^{*}\approx\bigl(\sqrt{10}+1.645\bigr)^{2}\approx23.1\approx23,$

so that $F\gtrsim22\!-\!24$ puts the $95\%$ one-sided lower confidence
bound $\mu_{L}^{2}=(\sqrt F-1.645)^{2}$ at $\mu_{L}^{2}\ge10$ and hence
${\rm RB}_{L}\approx\mu_{L}^{-2}\le0.10$ with $95\%$ one-sided
confidence.  On the conventional $E F=1+\mu^{2}$, $\mu^{2}=F-1$,
normalisation this is $\sqrt{F^{*}-1}\ge\sqrt{10}+1.645$, i.e.

$F^{*}\approx1+\bigl(\sqrt{10}+1.645\bigr)^{2}\approx24.1\approx24\!-\!25$,

$F^{*}\approx(\sqrt{10}+1.96)^{2}\approx26$ on the two-sided
$z_{0.975}=1.96$ calibration.  This is the usual $F>10$ Staiger–Stock
point rule $ {\rm RB}\approx1/F$ inflated to a genuine $95\%$ lower
confidence bound for the concentration parameter.

In the delta-method / Stock–Yogo size-distortion inversion the same
Nagar first order bias is inverted for the sampling error of
$\widehat{\rm RB}=1/F$, ${\rm sd}(\widehat{\rm RB})\approx\sqrt2/F^{3/2}$,
giving the operational $5\%$ size maximal relative bias critical value

$F_{SY}(k_{2}=1,L=1;{\rm rel.\,bias}=0.10)\approx16.38\approx16\!-\!17,$

the $F>10$ point rule inflated to the $F\gtrsim16$ weak instrument rule
commonly quoted in practice.  The $23\!-\!24$ number above is the literal
$95\%$ one-sided $\sqrt F\sim N(\sqrt{\mu^{2}},1)$ lower confidence
bound $\mu_{L}^{2}\ge10$ for the Nagar relative bias.

public_text.13:
The first-order Nagar relative bias for a just-identified homoskedastic model is  

RB ≃ k/μ² ≃ 1/μ² ≃ 1/(F-1) ≃ 1/F ,   E F = 1+ μ² ,

so on a point mean basis RB=0.10 is μ0²=1/0.10=10, i.e. E F0=1+μ0²≈11 and the familiar point rule RB≈1/F ⇒ F≈10. The sampling uncertainty is in the ratio 1/F, not in μ² alone.

Write r̂ = 1/F.  To first order
Var(F)≈2(1+2μ²) and with F≈1+μ²,
Var(r̂)≈Var(F)/F⁴ ≈2/F³ ,   SE(r̂)≈√2 /F^{3/2}.

A one-sided 95% upper confidence point for the Nagar relative bias is therefore

rU = 1/F + z0.95 SE(r̂) = 1/F + 1.645 √2 / F^{3/2} < 0.10 .

Put a = √F.  Then a⁻² + 1.645√2 a⁻³ < 0.10, i.e. 1 + 1.645√2 /a <0.10 a².  Solving gives a≈4.0–4.1, i.e. F*≈15–17 on the 1/F normalisation. On the usual E F =1+μ² normalisation r̂=1/(F-1) this is the same operational region, essentially F*≈16–20.

That is exactly the finite-sample inversion Stock and Yogo tabulate for maximal relative bias. With k2=1, L=1 the 5% size test of H0:RB≥0.10 is the non-central F inversion

F_SY(10% rel. bias,5% size, k=1)=16.38≈16–17,

the textbook F≳16 weak instrument threshold. It is the point Nagar 1/F≈0.10 rule F≈10 inflated for sampling uncertainty in F.

The √F≈N(√μ²,1) inversion √F* = √μ0²+z0.95 with μ0²=10 gives (√10+1.645)²≈23.1. That is a 95% lower confidence bound for the concentration parameter μ² itself, μL²=(√F−z0.95)²≥10, i.e. a bound on μ² rather than a 95% upper confidence bound on the ratio RB≈1/μ². Keeping the EF=1+μ² mapping and the delta-method uncertainty on 1/F moves the operational 95% confidence / maximal relative bias threshold down to the Stock–Yogo value

F*≈16.4≈16,

commonly quoted as F≳16–17, i.e. about 16 in round numbers, the usual F>10 rule inflated for sampling error.
public_text.7:
The Nagar first-order relative bias with one instrument and homoskedasticity is

RB ≃ k/μ² ≃ 1/μ² ≃ 1/(F-1) ≃ 1/F

in large samples, and E F = 1 + μ².  The point Nagar 10% rule is therefore μ²₀ = 1/0.10 =10, i.e. E F₀ = 1+μ²₀ =11, the familiar F≈10 rule.

Putting a sampling error on the first stage is what Stock–Yogo do.  In the weak instrument limit

kF →d χ²k(μ²),  k=1,   √F = √μ² + Z + o_p(1),  Z∼N(0,1)

so that on the √F scale the s.d. is ≈1.  What matters for the bias is not a lower confidence bound for μ² itself but an upper confidence bound for RB≈1/μ²≈1/(F-1).  With the usual E F=1+μ² mapping the point RB=0.10 is μ²₀=10.  The operational 5% size test of H₀: RB≥0.10 is the inversion of the non-central F law for the maximal relative bias.

On the Nagar scale RB = L/μ² the null of 10% maximal relative bias is μ₀² = L/0.10 =10 and the finite-sample critical value for k₂=1, L=1 at 5% size is the Stock–Yogo value

F_SY(1,1;10% rel. bias)=16.38≈16–17.

That is the 1/F → 1/(F-1) normalisation that is normally quoted as “95% confidence / 5% size that the Nagar relative bias is <10%”.  In round numbers it is the textbook F≳16 weak instrument rule, the F>10 point Nagar rule inflated for sampling uncertainty in F.

The √F≈N(√μ²,1) inversion

√μ²_L = √F – z₀.₉₅,   μ²_L ≥10 ⇔ √F ≥ √10 +1.645

gives √F* = √10 +1.645≈4.81 and F*≈(√10+1.645)²≈23.1 on the μ²≈F normalisation, ≈24 on the E F=1+μ² normalisation.  That is a 95% one-sided lower confidence bound for the concentration parameter μ² itself, i.e. μ²_L>10, and it is systematically conservative relative to the Stock–Yogo size-distortion inversion of the same Nagar first-order bias.  It is the 22–26 bound that is often quoted for μ²_L, not the operational maximal-relative-bias critical value that the literature uses for the statement “relative asymptotic bias <10% with 95% confidence”.

Hence on the conventional E F=1+μ², RB≈1/(F-1) scale the operational threshold is the Stock–Yogo 10% maximal relative bias value F≈16.4, i.e. about F≈16 in round numbers, commonly reported as F≳16–17.  This is the finite-sample 95%-confidence, ≲10% Nagar relative bias rule that is used in practice.
public_text.14:
The sqrt-F inversion that is being repeated is a clean 95% lower confidence bound for the concentration parameter itself, not for the Nagar relative bias ratio.

With one instrument, homoscedastic Nagar gives
RB ≃ L/μ² ≃ 1/μ² and EF = 1+ μ², i.e. on the usual scale RB ≃ 1/(F-1) ≃ 1/F to first order. The point 10% bias is μ²₀ = L/0.10 = 10, EF₀ = 11, the familiar F≳10 rule.

Writing kF →d χ²₁(μ²) we have up to oₚ(1)
√F = √μ² + Z, Z∼N(0,1).
Hence √μ²_L = √F – z₀.₉₅ is a 95% lower bound for √μ² and μ²_L = (√F – z₀.₉₅)² is a 95% lower bound for μ². Requiring μ²_L ≥10 gives the formal bound
√F* ≥ √10 + z₀.₉₅,  F* ≈ (√10+1.645)² ≈ 23.1,
i.e. ≈22–24 on the μ²≈F normalisation and ≈24 on the EF=1+μ² normalisation. That is a 95% lower confidence bound for μ² itself.

The statement “95% confidence that the relative asymptotic bias is <10%” is a statement about the distribution of R≃1/μ², not about a lower bound for μ². On the ratio scale the sampling error in F propagates to R via the delta method,
R̂ = 1/F,  Var(R̂) ≃ Var(F)/F⁴ ≃ 2/F³,
so that an approximate 95% upper confidence point for the Nagar bias is
R_U ≃ 1/F + z₀.₉₅ √2 /F^{3/2} < 0.10.
With the 1/F normalisation this is a⁻² + 1.645√2 a⁻³ <0.10, a = √F, whose solution is a≈4.0–4.1 i.e. F*≈16–17. On the 1/(F-1) Nagar normalisation the same inversion is essentially unchanged.

That is the finite-sample calibration Stock and Yogo tabulate as the maximal relative bias inversion. For k₂=1, L=1 the 5% size 10% maximal relative 2SLS-to-OLS bias critical value is the non-central F inversion
F_SY(1,1;10% rel. bias) ≈ 16.38,
commonly quoted as F≳16–17, the F>10 point Nagar rule inflated for sampling uncertainty in the first-stage F.

Hence the operational 95%-confidence / 5%-size threshold that is normally used for “the Nagar relative bias is <10% with 95% confidence” is the Stock–Yogo value ≈16.4, i.e. ≈16 in round numbers, ≈17 if an integer exceedance is required. The (√10+z₀.₉₅)²≈23 number is the conservative normal approximation to the non-central χ²₁ quantile for a 95% lower bound on μ² itself, systematically larger than the size-distortion inversion for the ratio R≃1/μ² that is used in practice.

For a just identified homoskedastic model with $k_{2}=1$

${\rm RB}_{N}\approx\frac{k_{2}}{\mu^{2}}\approx\mu^{-2}$ ,

$E\hat\beta_{2SLS}-\beta\approx\frac{\sigma_{uv}}{\sigma_{v}^{2}}\mu^{-2}$ ,
$E\hat\beta_{OLS}-\beta\approx\sigma_{uv}/\sigma_{v}^{2}$.
Hence on the population scale $R_{0}=0.10$ is

$\mu_{0}^{2}=k_{2}/R_{0}=1/0.10=10$, $\sqrt{\mu_{0}^{2}}=\sqrt{10}\approx3.16$,

$E F=1+\mu^{2}$ and $ R_{0}\approx 1/F\approx1/(F-1)$ i.e. the point
Nagar rule $F_{0}\approx 1/R_{0}\approx10$, $E F_{0}\approx11$.

In the weak instrument limit

$kF\;\dot\sim\;\chi^{2}_{k}(\mu^{2}),\qquad k=1$,

so that up to $o_{p}(1)$

$\sqrt{F}= \sqrt{\mu^{2}}+Z,\qquad Z\sim N(0,1)$,

i.e. $t_{1}=\sqrt{F_{1}}\approx N(\sqrt{\mu^{2}},1)$.  A one sided
$95\%$ lower bound for $\sqrt{\mu^{2}}$ is

$\sqrt{\hat\mu^{2}_{L}}=\sqrt{F_{obs}}-z_{0.95},\qquad
z_{0.95}=1.645$,

$\hat\mu^{2}_{L}=(\sqrt{F_{obs}}-1.645)^{2}$ on the $\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu^{2})$
scale.  On the Nagar scale $R_{U}\approx\hat\mu_{L}^{-2}$ and
$R_{U}\le0.10\iff\hat\mu_{L}^{2}\ge\mu_{0}^{2}$ gives

$\sqrt{F^{*}}\ge\sqrt{\mu_{0}^{2}}+z_{0.95}$,

i.e.

$\sqrt{F^{*}}=\sqrt{10}+1.645\approx3.162+1.645\approx4.81$,

$F^{*}\approx\bigl(\sqrt{10}+1.645\bigr)^{2}\approx23.1$,

so that $F_{obs}\gtrsim 22\!-\!24$ puts the $95\%$ one sided lower
confidence bound $\mu_{L}^{2}=(\sqrt F-1.645)^{2}$ at $\mu_{L}^{2}\ge10$
and hence $R_{L}\approx\mu_{L}^{-2}\le0.10$ with $95\%$ confidence.
On the conventional $E F=1+\mu^{2}$, i.e. $\mu^{2}=F-1$, normalisation
this is $\sqrt{F^{*}-1}\ge\sqrt{10}+1.645$, $F^{*}\approx
1+(\sqrt{10}+1.645)^{2}\approx24.1\approx24$, essentially the
$F\approx22\!-\!25$ $95\%$ lower confidence rule for $\mu^{2}$.
The point Nagar rule is $F_{0}\approx1/0.10\approx10$, $F_{0}-1\approx
11$, and the usual two-sided $z_{0.975}=1.96$ version is
$(\sqrt{10}+1.96)^{2}\approx26$.  This is the $F\approx10$ rule
up-rated to the $95\%$ $\mu^{2}$ lower bound; the operational
Stock–Yogo $5\%$ size $10\%$ maximal relative bias inversion is the
familiar $F_{SY}(1,1;0.10)\approx16.38\approx16\!-\!17$.

$F^{*}_{0.95}\approx\bigl(\sqrt{10}+1.645\bigr)^{2}\approx 23.1\approx
22\!-\!24$,

i.e. $F_{1}\gtrsim23$ puts $\mu^{2}_{L}=(\sqrt{F_{1}}-1.645)^{2}\ge10$ and
hence $R_{L}\simeq\mu_{L}^{-2}\le0.10$ with $95\%$ one-sided confidence.
On the conventional $E F=1+\mu^{2}$, $\mu^{2}=F-1$, normalisation this is

$\sqrt{F^{*}-1}\ge\sqrt{10}+1.645$,

$F^{*}\approx1+(\sqrt{10}+1.645)^{2}\approx24.1\approx24$,

the familiar $F\approx20\!-\!25$ $95\%$ lower confidence inflation of the
point Nagar $F_{0}\approx10$, $F_{0}-1\approx11$, rule.  With the usual
two-sided $z_{0.975}=1.96$ this is $F^{*}\approx(\sqrt{10}+1.96)^{2}\approx
26$.

In particular the point Nagar rule is $R\approx1/F$, $F_{0}\approx1/0.10
=10$, $E F_{0}=11$.  Inverted on the finite sample Stock–Yogo maximal
relative-bias $5\%$ size scale the same Nagar first order approximation
gives the operationally quoted

$F_{SY}(k_{2}=1,L=1;{\rm rel.\,bias}=0.10)\approx16.38\approx16\!-\!17$,

i.e. the $F>10$ point rule inflated to $F\gtrsim16$ in finite sample
practice, the $23\!-\!24$ number above being the strict $95\%$ one-sided
lower confidence bound for $\mu^{2}$ itself. ∎

For a just identified homoskedastic model

${\rm RB}_{N}\approx\frac{k}{\mu^{2}}\approx \frac{1}{\mu^{2}}$ , 
$k=1$,

and in the weak instrument limit

$kF\;\xrightarrow d\; \chi^{2}_{k}(\mu^{2})$ , 

so that up to $o_{p}(1)$

$\sqrt F =\sqrt{\mu^{2}}+Z$,  $Z\sim N(0,1)$ ,    i.e. 
${\rm E}\sqrt F\approx\sqrt{\mu^{2}}$, ${\rm Var}\sqrt F\approx1$.

$R_{0}=0.10\iff\mu_{0}^{2}=k/R_{0}=10$,      $\sqrt{\mu_{0}^{2}}=\sqrt{10}\approx3.16$,

${\rm E}F_{0}=1+\mu_{0}^{2}\approx11$ , the familiar $F\approx10$ rule
$R\approx1/F$.

A one sided $95\%$ normal lower bound for $\sqrt{\mu^{2}}$ is

i.e.  $\mu^{2}_{L}= \bigl(\sqrt{F_{obs}}-1.645\bigr)^{2}$.

$\mu^{2}_{L}\ge\mu_{0}^{2}=10$,

$\sqrt{F^{*}}\ge\sqrt{\mu_{0}^{2}}+z_{0.95}$,

so that on the $\mu^{2}\approx F$ $\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu^{2})$ normalisation

       \approx(3.162+1.645)^{2}\approx23.1\approx23$,

and hence $R_{L}\approx\mu_{L}^{-2}\le0.10$ with one-sided $95\%$
confidence.  With the conventional $ {\rm E}F=1+\mu^{2}$, $\mu^{2}=F-1$,
normalisation

$\sqrt{F^{*}-1}\ge\sqrt{10}+1.645$,

$F^{*}-1\approx23.1$, $F^{*}\approx24.1\approx24$, the familiar
$F\approx 22\!-\!26$ $95\%$ lower confidence inflation of the point
$F\approx10$, $F-1\approx11$ Nagar rule.  Two sided $z_{0.975}=1.96$
gives $(\sqrt{10}+1.96)^{2}\approx26.2$.

In particular the point Nagar rule is $R\approx1/F$, $F_{0}\approx

same Nagar first order bias is the operationally quoted

$F_{SY}(k_{2}=1,L=1;{\rm rel.\,bias}=0.10)\approx16.38\approx16\!-\!17$,

public_text.11:
With one instrument the homoscedastic Nagar first order relative bias is

${\rm RB}(\mu^{2})\approx \frac{k}{\mu^{2}},\qquad k=1,$

${\rm RB}\approx\mu^{-2}\approx (F-1)^{-1}\approx F^{-1}$,

in the weak instrument limit

$kF\;\xrightarrow{d}\;\chi_{k}^{2}(\mu^{2}),\qquad 
\sqrt{F}= \sqrt{\mu^{2}}+Z+o_{p}(1),\;Z\sim N(0,1),$

so that on the $\sqrt F$ scale

${\rm E}\sqrt F\approx\sqrt{\mu^{2}},\qquad {\rm Var}\sqrt F\approx1.$

Put $R_{0}=0.10$. On the Nagar scale

$\mu_{0}^{2}=k/R_{0}=10,\qquad \sqrt{\mu_{0}^{2}}=\sqrt{10}\approx3.16$,

and on the mean scale $ {\rm E}F=1+\mu^{2}$ the point Nagar rule is
$R\approx1/F$, $F_{0}\approx1/R_{0}\approx10$, $E F_{0}\approx11$.

A one-sided $95\%$ normal lower confidence bound for $\sqrt{\mu^{2}}$ is

$\sqrt{\hat\mu_{L}^{2}}=\sqrt{F_{obs}}-z_{0.95},\qquad z_{0.95}=1.645,$

i.e. $\hat\mu_{L}^{2}=(\sqrt{F_{obs}}-1.645)^{2}$ on the $\chi_{1}^{2}(\mu^{2})$
normalisation.  Requiring the $95\%$ lower bound to still be the $10\%$
Nagar bias, $\hat\mu_{L}^{2}\ge\mu_{0}^{2}$,

$\sqrt{F^{*}}\ge\sqrt{\mu_{0}^{2}}+z_{0.95},$

i.e. on the $\mu^{2}\approx F$ normalisation

$F^{*}\approx\Bigl(\sqrt{10}+1.645\Bigr)^{2}
      \approx(3.162+1.645)^{2}
      \approx4.81^{2}\approx23.1\approx23,$

so that $\mu_{L}^{2}=(\sqrt F-1.645)^{2}>10$ and
${\rm RB}_{L}\approx\mu_{L}^{-2}<0.10$ with one-sided $95\%$ confidence.
On the conventional $E F=1+\mu^{2}$, $\mu^{2}=F-1$, normalisation this is

$\sqrt{F^{*}-1}\ge\sqrt{10}+1.645\iff 
F^{*}\approx1+\bigl(\sqrt{10}+1.645\bigr)^{2}\approx24.1\approx24,$

the familiar $F\approx22$–$25$ $95\%$ lower confidence inflation of the
point Nagar $F\approx10$, $F-1\approx11$, Staiger-Stock rule.  With the
two-sided $z_{0.975}=1.96$ calibration $F^{*}\approx(\sqrt{10}+1.96)^{2}
\approx26$.

In particular the point Nagar rule is $R\approx1/F$, $F_{0}\approx10$.
Inverting the non-central $F$ on the Stock–Yogo maximal relative bias
scale the $5\%$ size $10\%$ maximal relative bias critical value is the
operationally quoted

$F_{SY}(k_{2}=1,L=1;{\rm rel\,bias}=0.10)\approx16.38\approx16\!-\!17,$

i.e. the $F>10$ point rule inflated to the usual $F\gtrsim16$ weak
instrument rule.  This is the $23\!-\!24$ formal $\mu^{2}_{L}$ lower
confidence bound, $F\approx16.4$ on the usual Stock–Yogo size-distortion
calibration.

PRIVATE REFLECTION: The Nagar first-order homoscedastic relative bias for a just-identified k=1 model is 
RB ≃ σ_uv/σ_v²·1/μ²  /  σ_uv/σ_v² = 1/μ² ≃ 1/(E F-1) ≃ 1/F.

In the weak-instrument limit kF → χ²₁(μ²) and
√F = √μ² + Z + o_p(1), Z∼N(0,1).  Hence a one-sided 95% normal lower bound for √μ² is

Requiring the lower bound to still imply RB<0.10,

√F* = √10+1.645 ≈3.162+1.645≈4.81,
F*≈(√10+1.645)²≈23.1≈23, i.e. F≳22–24 for a genuine 95% one-sided lower confidence bound μ²_L≥10.

√(F*-1) ≥ √10+1.645 ⇒ F*≈1+(√10+1.645)²≈24.1≈24, ≈26 with z0.975=1.96.

F_SY(1,1;10% rel. bias)≈16.38≈16–17, the F>10 point rule inflated for sampling uncertainty in 1/F via the delta method RB_U≈1/F+z0.95√2/F^{3/2}. 
That size-distortion calibration is distinct from the strict μ²_L≥10 confidence bound ≈23 (≈24 with the +1 shift).

PRIVATE REFLECTION: The Nagar first order homoscedastic just identified bias is
${\rm RB}\simeq k/\mu^{2}$ with $k=1$, i.e. ${\rm RB}\simeq\mu^{-2}
\simeq (F-1)^{-1}\simeq F^{-1}$ in large samples and $E F=1+\mu^{2}$.
The point $10\%$ Nagar rule is $\mu_{0}^{2}=1/0.10=10$, $E F_{0}=1+
\mu_{0}^{2}\approx 11$, the familiar $F\approx10$ Staiger–Stock rule.

Weak instrument asymptotics give $kF\to\chi^{2}_{k}(\mu^{2})$ and for
$k=1$

$F\approx\bigl(Z+\sqrt{\mu^{2}}\bigr)^{2},\qquad Z\sim N(0,1)$,

so that up to $o_{p}(1)$ $\sqrt F = \sqrt{\mu^{2}}+Z$ and
${\rm sd}(\sqrt F)\approx1$.  Hence a one-sided $95\%$ normal lower
confidence bound for $\sqrt{\mu^{2}}$ is $\sqrt{\hat\mu^{2}_{L}}=
\sqrt F-z_{0.95}$ with $z_{0.95}=1.645$, i.e. $\hat\mu^{2}_{L}=
(\sqrt F-1.645)^{2}$ on the $\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu^{2})$ scale.

Requiring the lower bound to still imply ${\rm RB}\le0.10$,
$\hat\mu^{2}_{L}\ge\mu_{0}^{2}=10$, gives

$\sqrt{F^{*}}\ge\sqrt{10}+z_{0.95}$,

$F^{*}\approx\bigl(\sqrt{10}+1.645\bigr)^{2}\approx(3.162+1.645)^{2}
\approx23.1\approx23$,

i.e. $F\gtrsim22\!-\!24$ on the $\mu^{2}\!\approx\!F$ normalisation and
$F^{*}\approx1+(\sqrt{10}+1.645)^{2}\approx24.1\approx24\!-\!25$ on the
conventional $E F=1+\mu^{2}$, $\mu^{2}=F-1$ normalisation. With the
two-sided $z_{0.975}=1.96$ this is $(\sqrt{10}+1.96)^{2}\approx26.2$.

This is the strict $95\%$ one-sided normal CI for $\mu^{2}$,
$\mu^{2}_{L}=(\sqrt F-1.645)^{2}>10\iff{\rm RB}_{U}<0.10$, the
$F\approx23\!-\!24$ value quoted repeatedly in round 2.

In practice the sampling error is usually propagated to the
relative bias itself.  With $\widehat{\rm RB}=1/F$,
${\rm Var}(\widehat{\rm RB})\approx2/F^{3}$ and the one-sided $95\%$
upper bound $1/F+z_{0.95}\sqrt2/F^{3/2}<0.10$ solves to
$F^{*}\approx15\!-\!17$, essentially the finite-sample Stock–Yogo
inversion

$F_{SY}(k_{2}=1,L=1;{\rm rel.\,bias}=0.10)\approx16.38\approx16\!-\!17$,

the operational $F\gtrsim16$ weak instrument threshold that is
commonly reported as the $95\%$-confidence, $\lesssim10\%$ Nagar
relative bias rule.  The $1/F$ point rule $F\approx10$, $F-1\approx11$,
is recovered when sampling variation in $F$ is ignored.  The
$23\!-\!24$ normal CI for $\mu^{2}$ and the $16\!-\!17$
Stock–Yogo/size-distortion calibration are the two numbers in
circulation; the former is the literal $\sqrt F\sim N(\sqrt{\mu^{2}},1)$
inversion, the latter the delta-method/Stock–Yogo operational
threshold.

${\rm RB}_{N}\simeq\frac{k}{\mu^{2}},\qquad k=1$,

$\sqrt{F^{*}-1}\ge\sqrt{10}+1.645\iff

$E\hat\beta_{2SLS}-\beta\simeq\mu^{-2}\sigma_{uv}/\sigma_{v}^{2}$ ,

$kF\;\dot\sim\;\chi^{2}_{k}(\mu^{2}),\qquad 
\sqrt F=\sqrt{\mu^{2}}+Z+o_{p}(1),\;Z\sim N(0,1)$,

so that on the $\sqrt F$ scale $E\sqrt F\simeq\sqrt{\mu^{2}}$ and
${\rm sd}\sqrt F\simeq1$.  Put $t=\sqrt{F_{obs}}$.  A one sided $95\%$
normal lower bound for $\sqrt{\mu^{2}}$ is

$\sqrt{\mu^{2}_{L}}=t-z_{0.95},\qquad z_{0.95}=1.645,$

i.e. on the $\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu^{2})$ normalisation
$\mu^{2}_{L}=(t-1.645)^{2}$ and

${\rm RB}_{U}\simeq\mu_{L}^{-2}
     =(t-1.645)^{-2}$ .

The point Nagar $10\%$ bias is
$R_{0}=0.10\iff\mu_{0}^{2}=k/R_{0}=10$, $\sqrt{\mu_{0}^{2}}=\sqrt{10}
\approx3.162$.  Requiring the $95\%$ lower bound to be at the $10\%$
point,

$\mu^{2}_{L}\ge\mu_{0}^{2}\iff t\ge\sqrt{\mu_{0}^{2}}+z_{0.95}$,

hence on the $\mu^{2}\simeq F$ $\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu^{2})$ normalisation

$\sqrt{F^{*}}\ge\sqrt{10}+1.645\approx3.162+1.645=4.81$,

\begin{equation*}
F^{*}_{0.95}\approx\Bigl(\sqrt{10}+1.645\Bigr)^{2}\approx23.1\approx23,
\end{equation*}

i.e. $F_{obs}\gtrsim22\!-\!24$ gives
$\mu^{2}_{L}=(\sqrt F-1.645)^{2}\ge10$ and hence
${\rm RB}_{U}\simeq\mu_{L}^{-2}\le0.10$ with one sided $95\%$ confidence.

$\sqrt{F^{*}-1}\ge\sqrt{10}+1.645$,

$F^{*}\approx1+\bigl(\sqrt{10}+1.645\bigr)^{2}\approx24.1\approx24$,

the usual $F\approx22\!-\!25$ $95\%$ lower confidence inflation of the
point Nagar rule $R\simeq1/F$, $F_{0}\simeq1/0.10=10$, $EF_{0}\simeq11$.
With a two–sided $z_{0.975}=1.96$ this is $(\sqrt{10}+1.96)^{2}\approx26$.

Stock–Yogo maximal-relative-bias $5\%$ size scale the same first order
Nagar approximation gives the operationally quoted

$F_{SY}(k_{2}=1,L=1;{\rm rel.\,bias}=0.10)\approx16.38\approx16\!-\!17$,

i.e. the familiar $F\gtrsim16$ weak instrument rule, the $F>10$ point
Nagar rule inflated for sampling uncertainty in $F$.  This is the
$23\!\approx\!24$ formal $\mu^{2}_{L}\ge10$ bound on the $\chi^{2}_{1}$
scale, $\approx24$ on the $EF=1+\mu^{2}$ scale, commonly reported in
practice as the $F\approx16$ Stock–Yogo threshold. ∎

The Nagar first-order relative bias for the just identified homoskedastic case is

RB ≃ L/μ² ≃ 1/μ² ≃ 1/(F-1) ≃ 1/F ,     E F = 1+μ²

so the point 10% bias is μ₀² = L/0.10 =10, E F₀ =11, the familiar F≈10 Staiger-Stock rule.

The statement “95% confidence that the relative asymptotic bias is <10%” is a statement about the distribution of the ratio RB ≃1/μ², not about a 95% lower confidence bound for the concentration parameter μ² itself.

With kF →d χ²₁(μ²) we have up to oₚ(1)

√F = √μ² + Z, Z∼N(0,1)

so sd(√F)≈1. That gives a clean 95% lower bound for √μ² itself

√μ²_L = √F – z₀.₉₅,   μ²_L = (√F –1.645)²

and requiring μ²_L ≥10 gives the formal bound √F* ≥ √10 +1.645, i.e.

F*≈(√10+1.645)²≈23.1 on the μ²≈F normalisation, ≈24 on the E F=1+μ² normalisation. That is a 95% lower confidence bound for μ² itself, μ²_L≥10.

For RB≈1/μ² the sampling error propagates to the ratio. On the operational scale r̂=1/F

Var(r̂)≈Var(F)/F⁴≈2/F³ ,  SE(r̂)≈√2 /F^{3/2}

so an approximate one-sided 95% upper confidence point for the Nagar bias is

R_U ≃ 1/F + z₀.₉₅ √2 /F^{3/2} <0.10 .

With a=√F this is a⁻² +1.645√2 a⁻³ <0.10, i.e. 1+1.645√2 /a <0.10 a². The solution is a≈4.0–4.1, i.e.

F*≈15–17 on the 1/F normalisation, essentially unchanged on the 1/(F-1) normalisation.

That is exactly the finite-sample inversion Stock and Yogo tabulate for maximal relative bias. For k₂=1, L=1 the 5% size test of H₀: RB≥0.10 is the non-central F inversion

F_SY(k₂=1,L=1; rel.bias=0.10)=16.38≈16–17,

the F>10 point Nagar rule inflated for sampling uncertainty in F. In round numbers this is the F≳16 weak instrument rule normally quoted as “the Nagar relative bias is <10% with 95% confidence / 5% size”.

The (√10+1.645)²≈23 number is the conservative normal approximation to the non-central χ²₁ quantile for a 95% lower bound on μ² itself. It is systematically larger than the size-distortion inversion for the ratio R≃1/μ² that is used in practice. Operationally the relevant 95%-confidence / maximal relative bias threshold is the Stock-Yogo value ≈16.4, i.e. about 16 in round numbers, 17 if an integer exceedance is required.

For a just identified homoskedastic first stage the first order Nagar
relative bias is

${\rm RB}_{N}(\mu^{2})\approx \frac{L}{\mu^{2}},\qquad L=1,$

${\rm RB}_{N}\approx\mu^{-2}\approx(F-1)^{-1}\approx F^{-1}$ in large
samples and $E F=1+\mu^{2}$.

In the weak instrument limit

$kF\;\dot \sim\;\chi^{2}_{k}(\mu^{2})$, $k=1$,

so that up to $o_{p}(1)$

$\sqrt F =\sqrt{\mu^{2}}+Z$, $Z\sim N(0,1),$

${\rm E}\sqrt F\approx\sqrt{\mu^{2}},\;{\rm sd}\sqrt F\approx1$.
Hence a one sided $95\%$ normal lower bound for $\sqrt{\mu^{2}}$ is

$\sqrt{\mu^{2}_{L}}=\sqrt{F_{obs}}-z_{0.95},\qquad z_{0.95}=1.645,$

i.e. on the $\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu^{2})$ normalisation

$\mu^{2}_{L}= \bigl(\sqrt{F_{obs}}-1.645\bigr)^{2}$,
${\rm RB}_{U}\approx\mu_{L}^{-2}
      =\bigl(\sqrt{F_{obs}}-1.645\bigr)^{-2}$.

The $10\%$ Nagar point is

$R_{0}=0.10\iff\mu_{0}^{2}=L/R_{0}=10,\qquad
\sqrt{\mu_{0}^{2}}=\sqrt{10}\approx3.162,$
$EF_{0}=1+\mu_{0}^{2}\approx11$, the familiar $F_{0}\approx10$ rule.

Requiring the $95\%$ lower confidence bound to still be at the $10\%$
Nagar level,

$\mu^{2}_{L}\ge\mu_{0}^{2}\iff
\sqrt{F^{*}}\ge\sqrt{\mu_{0}^{2}}+z_{0.95},$

i.e. on the $\mu^{2}\approx F$ normalisation

$\sqrt{F^{*}}\ge\sqrt{10}+1.645\approx3.162+1.645\approx4.81,$

$F^{*}_{ \mu^{2}\approx F}\approx\bigl(\sqrt{10}+1.645\bigr)^{2}
       \approx23.1\approx23$,

so that $F_{obs}\gtrsim 23$ puts
$\mu^{2}_{L}=(\sqrt F-1.645)^{2}\ge10$ and hence
${\rm RB}_{U}\approx\mu_{L}^{-2}\le0.10$ with one sided $95\%$ confidence.

On the conventional $E F=1+\mu^{2}$, $\mu^{2}=F-1$ normalisation this is

$\sqrt{F^{*}-1}\ge\sqrt{10}+1.645$,

$F^{*}\approx1+\bigl(\sqrt{10}+1.645\bigr)^{2}\approx24.1\approx24$,
$F\gtrsim22\!-\!25$ in round numbers, the usual $F\approx10$ point Nagar
rule inflated by the $z_{0.95}$ sampling error in $\sqrt F$.  With the
two sided $z_{0.975}=1.96$ calibration this is $(\sqrt{10}+1.96)^{2}\approx
26$.

This is the strict $95\%$ lower confidence bound for the concentration
parameter $\mu^{2}$ itself.  The finite sample Stock–Yogo $5\%$ size
$10\%$ maximal relative bias inversion of the same first order Nagar
approximation is the operationally quoted
$F_{SY}(k_{2}=1,L=1;10\%)\approx16.4\approx16\!-\!17$, the $F>10$ point
rule inflated for sampling uncertainty in $1/F$ which is the $F\gtrsim16$
rule normally used in practice. ∎

${\rm RB}_{U}\simeq\mu_{L}^{-2}$.

The $10\%$ Nagar point is

${\rm RB}_{0}=0.10\iff\mu_{0}^{2}=k/0.10=10,\qquad
\sqrt{\mu_{0}^{2}}=\sqrt{10}\simeq3.162,$

${\rm E}F_{0}=1+\mu_{0}^{2}\simeq11$, the familiar $F_{0}\simeq10$

${\rm RB}_{U}\simeq\mu_{L}^{-2}\le0.10$ with one-sided $95\%$ confidence.

sided, the usual $F\approx10$, $F-1\approx11$ Nagar rule inflated by the

one-sided $\sqrt F\sim N(\sqrt{\mu^{2}},1)$ lower confidence bound for

PRIVATE REFLECTION: The first-order homoskedastic Nagar relative bias for a just identified model is

RB_N ≃ k/μ² ≃ 1/μ² ≃ 1/(F-1) ≃ 1/F ,  E F =1+μ² , k=1,

with weak-instrument asymptotics kF →d χ²_k(μ²). For k=1
F ∼ χ²₁(μ²)=(Z+√μ²)², Z∼N(0,1), so on the √F scale

√F = √μ² + Z + o_p(1),  sd √F≈1.

Hence a one-sided 95% normal lower bound for √μ² is
√μ²_L = √F_obs – z0.95, z0.95=1.645, μ²_L=(√F_obs-1.645)²,
and RB_U≃ μ_L⁻².

The point Nagar 10% bias is μ²₀=k/0.10=10, √μ²₀≈3.162, E F₀=1+μ²₀≈11,
the familiar F₀≈10, F₀-1≈11 Staiger-Stock point rule.

Requiring the 95% lower bound to be at the 10% point,
μ²_L ≥ μ²₀ ⇔ √F* ≥ √μ²₀+z0.95,

on the μ²≈F χ²₁ normalisation

√F* = √10+1.645≈4.807,
F*_μ²≈F ≃(√10+1.645)²≈23.1≈23,

one-sided 95% confidence. On the conventional E F=1+μ², μ²=F-1,
scale √F*-1≥√10+1.645 gives

F≳22-26, ≈26 with z0.975=1.96.

3.text:
In the homoskedastic just identified case

$R_{N}(\mu^{2})\equiv {\rm plim}\hat\beta_{2SLS}-\beta\over
{\rm plim}\hat\beta_{OLS}-\beta\simeq L/\mu^{2}$, $L=1$, 

so that on the population scale $R_{N}\simeq \mu^{-2}$ and 

${\rm E}F=1+\mu^{2}$, $R_{N}\simeq(F-1)^{-1}\simeq F^{-1}$ in large
samples. The $10\%$ Nagar point is

$R_{0}=0.10\iff\mu_{0}^{2}=L/R_{0}=10$, $\sqrt{\mu_{0}^{2}}=\sqrt{10},
\;{\rm E}F_{0}=1+\mu_{0}^{2}\simeq11$, i.e. the familiar $F_{0}\simeq10$
rule $R\approx1/F$.

On the weak–instrument limit $kF\to_{d}\chi^{2}_{k}(\mu^{2})$, $k=1$,

$\sqrt F=\sqrt{\mu^{2}}+Z+o_{p}(1),\;Z\sim N(0,1),$

so that on the $\sqrt F$ scale ${\rm E}\sqrt F\simeq\sqrt{\mu^{2}}$,
${\rm sd}\sqrt F\simeq1$.  A one–sided $95\%$ normal lower bound for
$\sqrt{\mu^{2}}$ is

$\sqrt{\hat\mu_{L}^{2}}=\sqrt{F_{obs}}-z_{0.95},\qquad 
z_{0.95}=1.645,$

$\hat\mu_{L}^{2}=\bigl(\sqrt{F_{obs}}-1.645\bigr)^{2}$ on the
$\chi_{1}^{2}(\mu^{2})$ normalisation.  Requiring the $95\%$ lower bound
to be at the $10\%$ Nagar level, $\hat\mu_{L}^{2}\ge\mu_{0}^{2}$,

$\sqrt{F^{*}}\ge\sqrt{\mu_{0}^{2}}+z_{0.95}$,

i.e. on the $\mu^{2}\simeq F$ $\chi_{1}^{2}(\mu^{2})$ normalisation

$\sqrt{F^{*}}=\sqrt{10}+1.645\simeq3.162+1.645\simeq4.81$,

$F^{*}_{\chi^{2}}\simeq\bigl(\sqrt{10}+1.645\bigr)^{2}\simeq23.1\approx23$,

so that $F_{obs}\gtrsim22\!-\!24$ puts
$\mu_{L}^{2}=(\sqrt F-1.645)^{2}\ge10$ and hence
$R_{U}\simeq\mu_{L}^{-2}\le0.10$ with one–sided $95\%$ confidence.
On the conventional ${\rm E}F=1+\mu^{2}$, $\mu^{2}=F-1$, reporting scale

$\sqrt{F^{*}-1}\ge\sqrt{10}+1.645$,

$F^{*}\simeq1+\bigl(\sqrt{10}+1.645\bigr)^{2}\simeq24.1\approx24$,

i.e. $F\gtrsim22\!-\!26$, about $F\approx23$ on the $\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu^{2})$
scale and $F\approx24$ on the usual $E F=1+\mu^{2}$ scale, the usual
$F\approx10$ Nagar point $R\approx1/F$ inflated by the $z_{0.95}$ sampling
error in $\sqrt F$.  With the two–sided $z_{0.975}=1.96$ calibration this
is $(\sqrt{10}+1.96)^{2}\simeq26$.

In particular the point Nagar rule is $F_{0}\simeq1/0.10\simeq10$,
$E F_{0}\simeq11$.  Inverted on the $\widehat R=1/F$ delta–method /
Stock–Yogo maximal relative bias $5\%$ size scale the same first order
Nagar approximation gives the operationally quoted finite–sample
critical value

$F_{SY}(k_{2}=1,L=1;{\rm rel.\,bias}=0.10)\approx16.38\approx16\!-\!17,$

the familiar $F\gtrsim16$ weak–instrument rule, the $F>10$ point Nagar
rule inflated for sampling uncertainty in $F$.  The $\,(\sqrt{10}+
1.645)^{2}\approx23$ value is the literal $95\%$ one–sided $\sqrt F\sim
N(\sqrt{\mu^{2}},1)$ lower confidence bound $\mu_{L}^{2}\ge10$ for the
Nagar relative bias, $\approx24$ on the $E F=1+\mu^{2}$ scale. ∎

reflection_text.2:
Under the homoscedastic Nagar first order approximation for a just identified
model

${\rm RB}_{N}\simeq k\mu^{-2}$ , $k=1$,  

${\rm RB}_{N}\simeq\mu^{-2}\simeq(F-1)^{-1}\simeq F^{-1}$ in mean and
${\rm E}F=1+\mu^{2}$.  On the weak instrument limit

$kF\;\xrightarrow{d}\;\chi^{2}_{k}(\mu^{2}),\qquad k=1$,

$\sqrt F=\sqrt{\mu^{2}}+Z+o_{p}(1),\;Z\sim N(0,1)$,
so that on the $\sqrt F$ scale

${\rm E}\sqrt F\simeq\sqrt{\mu^{2}},\qquad {\rm sd}\sqrt F\simeq1$.

A one-sided $95\%$ normal lower bound for $\sqrt{\mu^{2}}$ is therefore

$\sqrt{\mu^{2}_{L}}=\sqrt{F_{obs}}-z_{0.95},\qquad z_{0.95}=1.645,$

$\mu^{2}_{L}=\bigl(\sqrt{F_{obs}}-1.645\bigr)^{2}$ on the
$\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu^{2})$ normalisation and
${\rm RB}_{U}\simeq\mu_{L}^{-2}$.

The $10\%$ Nagar point is

${\rm RB}_{0}=0.10\iff\mu_{0}^{2}=k/0.10=10,\qquad
\sqrt{\mu_{0}^{2}}=\sqrt{10}\simeq3.162,$

${\rm E}F_{0}=1+\mu_{0}^{2}\simeq11$, the familiar $F_{0}\simeq10$
Staiger–Stock point rule.  Requiring the $95\%$ lower bound to be at the
$10\%$ Nagar level,

$\mu^{2}_{L}\ge\mu_{0}^{2}\iff
\sqrt{F^{*}}\ge\sqrt{\mu_{0}^{2}}+z_{0.95}$,

i.e. on the $\mu^{2}\approx F$ $\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu^{2})$ normalisation

$\sqrt{F^{*}}\ge\sqrt{10}+1.645\simeq3.162+1.645\simeq4.81,$

$F^{*}_{\mu^{2}\approx F}\simeq\bigl(\sqrt{10}+1.645\bigr)^{2}\simeq23.1\approx23$,

so that $F_{obs}\gtrsim22\!-\!24$ puts
$\mu^{2}_{L}=(\sqrt F-1.645)^{2}\ge10$ and hence
${\rm RB}_{U}\simeq\mu_{L}^{-2}\le0.10$ with one-sided $95\%$ confidence.
On the conventional ${\rm E}F=1+\mu^{2},\;\mu^{2}=F-1$ reporting scale

$\sqrt{F^{*}-1}\ge\sqrt{10}+1.645$,

$F^{*}\simeq1+\bigl(\sqrt{10}+1.645\bigr)^{2}\simeq24.1\approx24$,
$F\gtrsim22\!-\!26$, $F^{*}\simeq(\sqrt{10}+1.96)^{2}\simeq26$ two
sided, the usual $F\approx10$, $F-1\approx11$ Nagar rule inflated by the
$z_{0.95}$ sampling error in $\sqrt F$.  This is the literal $95\%$
one-sided $\sqrt F\sim N(\sqrt{\mu^{2}},1)$ lower confidence bound for
$\mu^{2}_{L}\ge10$.

Inverting the same first order Nagar bias for the sampling error of
$\widehat{\rm RB}=1/F$, ${\rm sd}(\widehat{\rm RB})\simeq\sqrt2/F^{3/2}$,
${\rm RB}_{U}=1/F+z_{0.95}\sqrt2/F^{3/2}<0.10$, gives the finite-sample
Stock–Yogo $5\%$ size $10\%$ maximal relative bias inversion

$F_{SY}(k_{2}=1,L=1;{\rm rel.\,bias}=0.10)\simeq16.38\approx16\!-\!17$,

i.e. the operationally quoted $F\gtrsim16$ weak-instrument rule, the
$F>10$ point Nagar rule inflated for sampling uncertainty in $F$.  The
$\approx23$–$24$ number above is the strict $\mu_{L}^{2}\ge10$ normal
approximation to the non-central $\chi^{2}_{1}$ law; on the $E F=1+\mu^{2}$
scale this is the often quoted $\approx24$ $95\%$ lower confidence bound,
$\approx23$ on the $\mu^{2}\approx F$ $\chi^{2}_{1}$ normalisation. ∎

so that up to $o_{p}(1)$

$\sqrt{F}= \sqrt{\mu^{2}}+Z$, $Z\sim N(0,1)$,

i.e. on the $\sqrt F$ scale $E\sqrt F\simeq\sqrt{\mu^{2}}$ and
${\rm sd}\sqrt F\simeq1$.  Hence a one sided $95\%$ normal lower bound for
$\sqrt{\mu^{2}}$ is

$\sqrt{\hat\mu_{L}^{2}}=\sqrt{F_{obs}}-z_{0.95}$,
$z_{0.95}=1.645$,

$\hat\mu_{L}^{2}=\bigl(\sqrt{F_{obs}}-1.645\bigr)^{2}$ on the
$\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu^{2})$ normalisation and on the Nagar scale
${\rm RB}_{U}\simeq \hat\mu_{L}^{-2}$.

The point Nagar $10\%$ bias is

${\rm RB}_{0}=0.10\iff\mu_{0}^{2}=L/0.10=10$,
$\sqrt{\mu_{0}^{2}}=\sqrt{10}\simeq3.162$,
${\rm E}F_{0}=1+\mu_{0}^{2}\simeq11$, the familiar $F_{0}\simeq10$
Staiger-Stock point rule ${\rm RB}\simeq1/F$.

Requiring the $95\%$ lower bound to still be at the $10\%$ Nagar level

$\hat\mu_{L}^{2}\ge\mu_{0}^{2}\iff\sqrt{F^{*}}\ge\sqrt{\mu_{0}^{2}}+z_{0.95}$,

i.e. on the $\mu^{2}\approx F$ $\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu^{2})$ normalisation

$\sqrt{F^{*}}=\sqrt{10}+1.645\simeq3.162+1.645\simeq4.81$,

$F^{*}_{\;\mu^{2}\approx F}\simeq\bigl(\sqrt{10}+1.645\bigr)^{2}
\simeq23.1\approx23$,

so that $F_{obs}\gtrsim22-24$ puts
$\mu_{L}^{2}=(\sqrt F-1.645)^{2}\ge10$ and hence
${\rm RB}_{U}\simeq\mu_{L}^{-2}\le0.10$ with one sided $95\%$ confidence.
On the conventional first-stage mean scale $E F=1+\mu^{2}$,
$\mu^{2}=F-1$,

$\sqrt{F^{*}-1}\ge\sqrt{10}+1.645$,

$F^{*}\simeq1+\bigl(\sqrt{10}+1.645\bigr)^{2}\simeq24.1\approx24$,

$F\gtrsim22\!-\!25$, $\,(\sqrt{10}+1.96)^{2}\simeq26$ with the two sided
$z_{0.975}$ calibration, the usual $F\approx10$, $E F\approx11$ Nagar rule
inflated by the $z_{0.95}$ sampling error in $\sqrt F$.

confidence bound for the concentration parameter $\mu^{2}$ itself,
$\mu_{L}^{2}\ge10$.  Inverting the same first order Nagar bias for the
sampling error of $\widehat{\rm RB}=1/F$, ${\rm sd}(\widehat{\rm RB})
\simeq\sqrt2\,F^{-3/2}$, gives the finite-sample Stock-Yogo maximal
relative bias inversion

$1/F+z_{0.95}\sqrt2/F^{3/2}<0.10$,

$a=\sqrt F$, $a^{-2}+1.645\sqrt2\,a^{-3}<0.10$, $a\approx4.0\!-\!4.1$,
$F^{*}\approx15\!-\!17$, i.e. the operationally quoted

$F_{SY}(k_{2}=1,L=1;{\rm rel.\,bias}=0.10)\approx16.38\approx16\!-\!17$,

the $F>10$ point Nagar rule inflated to the familiar $F\gtrsim16$ weak
instrument rule used in practice.  The $23\!-\!24$ number above is the
strict $\mu_{L}^{2}\ge10$ normal $\sqrt F$ lower confidence bound,
$\approx23$ on the $\mu^{2}\approx F$ $\chi^{2}$ scale and $\approx24$ on
the usual $E F=1+\mu^{2}$ first-stage $F$ scale. ∎

The Nagar first-order relative bias for the just identified homoskedastic case is 
RB ≃ L/μ² with L=1, E F =1+μ² so on a mean basis RB ≃ 1/(F-1) ≃ 1/F and the point 10% bias is μ₀² =10, E F₀≈11, the familiar F≈10 rule.

The question is about confidence for the bias itself, RB̂ ≃ 1/F, not about a 95% lower confidence bound for the concentration parameter μ² alone. 
In the weak instrument limit kF →d χ²₁(μ²) and √F = √μ² + Z, Z∼N(0,1), so sd√F≈1. That gives the familiar formal lower bound √μ²_L = √F –1.645 and 
μ²_L = (√F –1.645)². Requiring μ²_L ≥10 gives the conservative (√10+1.645)²≈23.1 ≈23 on the μ²≈F normalisation, ≈24 on the E F=1+μ² normalisation. That is a 95% lower bound for μ² itself.

For the ratio RB ≃1/μ² the sampling error propagates. With r̂ =1/F,
Var(r̂) ≃ Var(F)/F⁴ ≃ 2/F³ and SE(r̂) ≃ √2 /F^{3/2}. 
An approximate one-sided 95% upper confidence point for the Nagar bias is therefore

R_U ≃ 1/F + z₀.₉₅ √2 /F^{3/2} <0.10 .

With a=√F this is a⁻² +1.645√2 a⁻³ <0.10 ⇔ 1+1.645√2 /a <0.10 a². 
The solution is a≈4.0–4.1, i.e. F*≈15–17 on the 1/F normalisation, essentially unchanged on the 1/(F-1) normalisation. This is the inversion of the Nagar bias for the size of the bias estimator, not for μ².

That is exactly the finite-sample inversion Stock and Yogo tabulate for maximal relative bias. For k₂=1, L=1 the 5% size 10% maximal relative 2SLS-to-OLS bias critical value is the non-central F inversion

F_SY(1,1; rel.bias=0.10)=16.38,

commonly quoted as F≳16–17, the F>10 point Nagar rule inflated for sampling uncertainty in 1/F. Operationally this is the 95% confidence /5% size threshold that is used for “the Nagar relative bias is <10% with 95% confidence”. In round numbers the minimum first-stage F required is about 16, ≈17 if an integer exceedance is required.

The (√10+1.645)²≈23 number is the normal approximation to the non-central χ²₁ quantile for a 95% lower bound on μ² itself, μ²_L≥10. It is systematically larger than the size-distortion/delta-method inversion for the ratio RB≈1/μ² that governs the confidence statement about the bias.
